t: Why We Said ‘No’ to IVF and ‘Yes’ to Embryo Adoption
q: By God’s grace, in 2019 I spent hours during our last year of seminary researching and writing about infertility, assisted reproductive technologies, and the ethical issues surrounding their use. At the time, I thought of this as my latest theological hobbyhorse. It was interesting and important to me, but it wasn’t personal.

For those with children or loved ones conceived via IVF, these critiques feel deeply personal. Yet I want to make clear that critiques of IVF have nothing to do with the value and dignity of children conceived via IVF.

If pro-life Christians agree that a unique human life begins at fertilization, then just as early-term abortion that kills an embryo inside the womb is wrong, destroying embryos developed outside the womb is wrong. If couples who conceive naturally shouldn’t abort a pregnancy because the baby has a genetic disorder, then embryos created via IVF shouldn’t be destroyed for the same reason.
Unlike in IVF, no new children are created through embryo adoption. Rather, a child who already exists gets a chance to live and be part of a family.

It’s possible to lament the broken circumstances that led to the child’s need for adoption while also rejoicing in the gift of becoming that child’s parents—as parents of traditionally adopted children do.

The average success rate for a donor embryo transfer is between 43 percent and 45 percent, a discouraging prospect. We’re so grateful that our first embryo transfer led to the healthy birth of our daughter, but we were mentally prepared for the prospect of multiple failed transfers.

As with traditional adoption, these children are likely to have confusing feelings about their origin stories and questions about their genetic parents that may be difficult or impossible for their adoptive parents to answer.
Infertility taught me that protection from suffering isn’t guaranteed in the Christian life. In fact, suffering with and for Jesus is promised.

t: When Your Leader Tells You to Part Ways With One of Your Direct Reports
q: Making the case that this team member is better than the leader believes, or that they have institutional knowledge or relationships that make them hard to replace, will rarely change the leader’s mind. At best, it usually results in the leader declaring it is your call, but that they still advise you to make a change at some point soon.

The wrong strategy is to ignore this advice and hope the team member can redeem themselves at some point. If you’re going to hang on to this team member despite your leader’s recommendation, you need a plan.
The plan starts with candor in both directions. Go back to your leader with a specific timeline and the observable markers of improvement you will be tracking. Vague reassurances don’t cut it.

They need to know in concrete terms exactly what performance or behavior triggered this scrutiny and what closing the gap requires. Protecting the team member without telling them they need protecting only delays the inevitable and almost always ends poorly.

q: None of this is visible in the way that asking a question, making a prediction, or stopping to summarize is visible. And therein lies the fatal instructional mistake that has held back reading achievement for decades: We observed what good readers do and tried to teach struggling readers to imitate those behaviors, while paying far less attention to what good readers know.
Students judged to be “poor readers” who knew a lot about baseball substantially outperformed ostensibly “good readers” who knew little about the game.
It’s not quite right to say that background knowledge improves reading comprehension. That makes knowledge sound like an enhancement—a helpful supplement that makes reading somewhat easier.

Two children can sit through the same lesson or read the same book and emerge having learned different amounts—not because one is more intelligent or attentive, but because one had more knowledge available to make sense of the new material.

This is why the familiar conflict between teaching knowledge and teaching children “how to think” is misconceived. Knowledge does not crowd out higher-order thinking. It’s what makes higher-order thinking possible.

Every additional hour spent practicing finding the main idea, making connections, and identifying an author’s purpose is an hour that is lost learning about the solar system, ancient civilizations, ecosystems, mythology, music, art, and literature—the knowledge that will make future texts more comprehensible.

If knowledge compounds, then a genuinely knowledge-rich education must compound too. A coherent curriculum should build deliberately and cumulatively from year to year. No individual teacher can create that coherence alone.
Reading comprehension is not principally a skill we teach. It is a condition we create. And we create it by teaching children about the world.

t: They Just Wanna Be Loved
q: Every kid is different. Every kid likes different things. But what they all have in common is that they want stuff.
Lots of it. Toys and attention. Affection and confections. Excitement…and expenses.
But you know what they really want, above anything else—even more than the stuff they ask for?
They want to know they’re enough. They want to know they are safe. They want to know you’re proud of them.
At the core of it, they just wanna be loved. By you—by their parents.
There is nothing else they want more and no one else they want it from more. So don’t hold it back.

q: This is not an attempt to criticize them —I also thought that way until very recently—, but rather something I have been observing ever since I decided to propose to my girlfriend, and that is that the average male believes marriage requires a long list of things that need to happen before it’s a sensible decision to commit to a woman for life, instead of seeing it as the foundation of stability and real progress.

Not ready” usually means —beneath the surface— fear of permanent commitment, attachment to the perceived freedom of choice of single life, and the comfortable lie that there exists a point in the future when you’ll feel fully prepared, fully in control, and fully secure to make a choice and commitment of this magnitude.
The issue, in short, is that a man who says he’s not ready at 29 (with some exceptions), will rarely be ready at 35, he’ll just be older and more used to postponing.

Consider the logic of it: if two people have spent 15 years learning to be alone, devising perfect routines for themselves, and getting attached to the way they do things, it will be much more difficult for them to create a life together.

t: Student AI Use Is About Much More Than School Rules
q: It took well over a decade to see the alarming impact of smartphones, social media, and school-issued devices on children, and longer still to demand action to protect students from harmful effects. We clearly can’t wait that long on AI.

In addition to increasingly clear impacts on learning, AI use raises complex questions about honesty, judgment, and whether struggling through difficult work has inherent value separate from the final product. Parents who believe a child’s moral education starts at home need to engage in conversations about when and how—or if—the technology should be used.

For my youngest child, in her last year of elementary school, teachers seem noticeably more cautious about technology in their classrooms. Instead of seeking out ways to incorporate tech, they ask whether the task works without it.

Action on screen time, driven by consensus, is a welcome development. Yet limiting the number of minutes a child spends on their school-issued device does not resolve the difficult questions—more moral than technical—that come with an AI future.
Students may earn better grades for less work, but a recent analysis of closed-book test scores confirms that students using AI are not obtaining knowledge along the way.
And even if kids want to avoid AI, their perceptions of peer use mean that every assignment brings a moral reckoning over whether the cost to not use AI is too high.

Pressing “pause” on AI in schools is necessary but insufficient. Today’s students will not know a world without this new technology, and it’s up to the adults in their lives to equip them with the human capacity to debate and decide how it should be used.

t: Mental Models and Professional Development
q: The paper finds that there is a relative lack of coherence about how best to surface, change and support teachers’ mental models. This means that while we have methods that help us to do these three elements, we don’t yet understand how they interact together especially well.

I find this so interesting because it reminds us that mental models help to bring structure to what is naturally an ill-structured system. Where the lack of structure in the system means that so much is dependent on how situations are interpreted and how teachers act on that interpretation, it makes a strong case for mental models being central to how we understand the effectiveness of teaching.

I think that it is far less common for professional learning to consider assumptions and beliefs that teachers bring to situations. So, if we accept that mental models lead to the decisions we make in the classroom and therefore they tell us a lot about teaching quality, we are potentially missing a trick if we don’t deliberately surface, examine and develop assumptions and beliefs.

I can’t have the same success rate with changing beliefs and assumptions, partly because they tend to be more varied within a group than knowledge and partly because people tend to hold onto beliefs and assumptions more tightly than knowledge – they feel more personal. It is also much more difficult to surface assumptions and beliefs than knowledge.

Of course, in the busy and fast paced reality of school life, it is easy to slip into focusing on the actions and allowing our feedback to focus on the correction of teaching moves rather than on the making of meaning that drove the decision to use that teaching move.

Beliefs are particularly important to teachers because, like many vocational professions, there is a moral drive behind many peoples’ decision to enter it. t: How To Find God In A Five Cent Fruit
q: Civilization is strange. We removed the burden of nature only to find a far greater burden—the burden of freedom from nature.

First, a chronic desire for the next moment: the next vacation, promotion, phone, or blissful image in our skull of a perfect future, and all we need to do to earn it is be miserable just a little while longer… or so we tell ourselves. And second, to keep this desire active, the malady demands a willful blindness to a cosmic truth—what we are seeking over there already exists right here.
The act of stopping and putting ink to paper cuts everything else away but the singular object of our focus for the briefest of moments.
And yet… the astronomical difference between these two types of grapes is as nothing compared to the difference between the grapes and everything else we could be thinking about as we eat them.
What is Epictetus telling us? That our desire to be somewhere else is in fact a confession we are not content to be ourselves.
It seems we are born with a simple choice: we may make of ourselves slaves to relative comparisons, or we can choose to be free men and women in obedience to the creed of absolute awe.

We crave to bring our vision of the future to reality, and yet once we get it, suddenly it is worthless, and it becomes a mere stepping stone to a better vision of the future. It is a bitter irony that it is a vision we may never even live to see.

This is not a call to abandon the future and live a life of low standards. Far from it. Rather, it is to learn to love a paradox: the only way to be satisfied with an extraordinary future, which will itself become the everyday, is to be extraordinarily satisfied with the everyday.

t: How Normal People are Blowing Up All Over the Internet
q: There’s nothing like walking out of the house you hate, de-icing your car at 6 am to drive 60 minutes to a job that sucks the life out of you, to push you to think about what else you could be doing.

But my problem wasn’t my job. It was that I wasn’t doing something that I had control over. That allowed me to be free and create. Fulfilment would come, I would find, through creation on my own terms — and that didn’t mean quitting, it just meant carving out time for creation.

You don’t have to spend hours trying to curate the perfect idea (whatever that means). Just start with what you’ve recently consumed and write your take on it. That’s it. Keep it simple. There’s a reason you are drawn to the things you consume, so create from them.

The worst thing you can do is write something or film something and expect it to go viral. It won’t, and you’ll feel like you’ve done it completely wrong. You haven’t. Virtually everyone starts with nobody watching. The benefit of nobody watching is that there are fewer people cringing at your early work.

And honestly, in the beginning you’ll suck, and you’ll be cringey. That is the price you pay for starting. And honestly, honestly, nobody cares. Not really. The person who cares the most about the cringey stuff you put out will be you. So get started, be a cringe-pot; in 365 days, you’ll be 100x better than you are today.

Humans were meant to build stuff, to solve problems, and to ponder. The problem is that we have so much input (social media, news, apps, etc.) that all that information has nowhere to go, and we internally combust.
I was fed up with constantly making promises that I never kept. Writing was the first time I said I was going to do something and actually did. That then became a habit.

Writing on the internet was never about going viral, making loads of money, or any of that stuff. It was about becoming the version of myself I wanted to become. The person who says they will and does.

t: How Long Are Students Really Engaged?
q: More than 30 years in classrooms taught me something different, and the research increasingly supports it. There is no fixed amount of time a student can or will remain engaged.

A student might stay deeply focused for twenty minutes during one activity and drift within minutes during another. Difficulty, working-memory demands, emotion, movement, classroom interaction, prior success, and what happened just before the task could all change what I saw.
Or are their eyes wandering? Am I seeing blank stares? Is work slowing down? Are conversations beginning? Are bodies getting restless?
I learned that sometimes what looked like defiance, frustration, or withdrawal was really a sign that I needed to change something.

If working memory seemed overloaded, I could review, record, talk it through, or break the information into smaller pieces. If the work had become too difficult, I could scaffold before frustration became disengagement or anger.
The learning goal did not have to change. I did not have to make the thinking easier. But the way students were engaging with the learning could.

t: Your Course Is Their Cosmos
q: I accepted the authority of the teacher’s roll call without thinking. I liked it. To know that there was a set of superior creations, and that I would read some of them was an assurance. I was 16, curious but uncertain, and here was a ranking of things I could trust.

He took his time, no rushing through the items, as if each figure and book deserved a pause. As the list grew, a bigger picture began to form, not one thing followed by another, but a lineage with each writer and work occupying a place in the whole. This was the American heritage, the Great American Novel.

At that point, having transcribed 80 years of canonical fiction, we could no longer regard the works he put on the syllabus as a casual matter of the teacher’s taste. For the next nine months, we’d be served a slice of an exclusive tradition, some of the best but not all. It made each novel more important. The plights of Henry Fleming, Frederic Henry, and Quentin Compson were personal to me, it turned out, and to believe that they marked special moments in American literary history enhanced my identification. Reading each work became a noble and fateful endeavor.

The courses presented a tiny model of or outlook upon time and being. They told me that the past contains momentous objects that fall into a plot. The implication was inescapable in courses that assigned materials from long ago that laid claim to greatness and influence.

I believe that such conclusions are drawn by students all the time. Whether a teacher intends it or not, the syllabus in any course with a historical or aesthetic dimension implies a picture of reality.

In my 11th Grade class, with a canon of masterful writings in hand, I learned that there is significance in the course of human events, that a record of achievement is waiting to be learned. Another syllabus, one without chronological order and that mixed pop culture with classics, might have led me to the opposite beliefs.

What a contrast that outlook is to the experience pressed upon the 15-year-old of today by media of all kinds, social and entertainment. What comes through the small and large screen amounts to a swarm of images, chatter, music, voices, videos, photos, sports highlights, celebrity profiles, games, and youth news. It’s a blooming, buzzing confusion that has no depth, no history, no rational sequence. A youth flooded with media easily assumes that existence itself is equally unstable and unstructured and indifferent to quality.

A humanistic course that puts superb materials into a coherent narrative with purpose and momentum can curb the unease. When teachers craft their syllabi, they should ask, “What am I implying about the universe? What am I saying about the past? Am I handing them a world that they shall be eager to join?” The implicit outlook of a course that puts the greats into a grand narrative can be a worthy antidote to the chaos that engulfs them the moment they leave the school grounds.

t: You're Running Out of Time
q: In De Brevitate Vitae, On The Shortness of Life- Seneca begins the essay with a bold accusation. Most of us live as if we’re immortal. We’re under the illusion that we’re entitled to all the time in the world.

We keep postponing reading the book, joining the run club, starting a business, going on that road trip, apologizing to the person we wronged, having that difficult conversation- because we assume we can always do it later.
Seneca thought otherwise. He said life is long enough if we know how to use it well.
Marcus Aurelius had an interesting way to think of this reality. He told himself to think of his life as done and whatever remained as extra.
Imagine you were told that you had one year left. What becomes embarrassing to continue caring about? Who would you call? What would you stop tolerating?

Ask if you’d love to spend one of your final moments with this person before staying in the wrong relationship for another year. Ask how many more mornings you assume the universe owes you before postponing the project again.
Also, other than prompting you into action, thinking of death helps you re-administer taste, enjoyment and value to ordinary life.
And usually, you won’t know it’s the last time while it’s happening. This should change how you participate in your life. You’re not getting another one.

t: Why Adult Children Are Cutting Off Their Parents
q: Gone are the days when family estrangement was a desperate, last resort of children who suffered through years of abuse and neglect under volatile, violent caregivers. In increasing numbers, adult children are disowning their parents, cutting off all communication and refusing any attempt at reconciliation, over nothing more serious than differences in political opinions.

When young adults break off contact with their families, it often imposes a huge emotional toll on the basis of seemingly minor infractions. One man cut his mother off because he suspected she voted for the wrong candidate. Another woman stopped communicating with her father because he was insufficiently enthusiastic about her sister’s gender transition.

Historically, “trauma” referred to serious psychological injury resulting from “extraordinary, catastrophic events like combat or surviving a train crash.” People now use the term to describe the discomfort experienced due to “political differences or unmet emotional needs” (18–19). Unpleasant but normal childhood experiences are now being labeled “trauma” and used to justify disowning parents. Though claims of trauma may seem exaggerated, they’re deemed indisputable because they’re validated as a person’s lived experience.

The cultural deconstruction of the family also plays a role in people’s willingness to sever connections. The family isn’t seen as a source of identity, growth, and stability but as a site of constraint, conformity, and oppression. Amid a culture seeking unbridled autonomy and individual self-expression, the family is a scandalous affront to one’s absolute sovereignty.

t: We're Getting Death Threats for Resisting EdTech
q: The same harms, problematic content, excessive use, and degradation of focus, empathy, and critical thinking skills that we hear about occurring on platforms like Snapchat and Meta are occurring on the internet-connected 1:1 devices and EdTech products used by over 90% of American schoolchildren.
These students are engaged in “reading.” There are no books on their desks. Instead, they are wearing headphones and plugged into iPads, on which they swipe digital “pages” to advance the “book.

Recently, an IT professional with 20 years of experience, whose role is to set up computers for corporate professionals, told me she was absolutely appalled by what she saw in the Chromebook that came home with her child– a lack of regulation and oversight that would never be permitted in a corporate workplace.

And families who have restricted their children’s use of screens before entering school are horrified to learn the iPad the school sent home has access to apps and websites they never would have approved. It’s hard to argue this is a “parenting” problem when these devices are provided by the school.

Just like we test the brakes on a car before we send it to the dealership; just like we perform trials before giving medication to the wider population; we must ask whether these products are safe, legal, effective, and better than the teacher they are clearly intended to replace.

My colleagues and I are not opposed to technology. We support computer labs with trained instructors, technology education programs (vs. EdTech products), and even the occasional use of digital tools that offer something an analog approach cannot.

EdTech products do not function without the internet, and to operate fully, they require significantly more broadband than what’s needed for a simple internet search, email, or typing class. Programs like eRate are being taken advantage of to benefit companies whose products won’t run on anything but “premium” levels of broadband, when a lower level would suffice for teacher and staff needs.

q: What Descartes was doing is what we call methodological skepticism: he was using doubt strategically to help him arrive at a certainty about the world. This practice has commonly been translated in modern speak to mean: “question everything”.
There is an important distinction here: Kids don’t simply experience new technologies or social changes differently. They inherit as normal what previous generations experienced as change.

And this is why my initial advice of “question everything” might have felt so compelling. It gives us permission to remain suspicious without ever deciding what deserves our belief; because it is easier to default to doubt than struggle for truth.

We need trust in expertise and institutions for society to continue functioning. Scepticism can give us good reasons to withdraw that trust, but on its own it tells us very little about where we should place it instead. Questioning the scientist doesn’t make the podcaster more reliable.

The natural response to this is to make more evidence more readily available so we can judge the science ourselves. But more information doesn’t mean better judgment. O’Neill explains that information only helps if people can assess what they’re looking at.

We have been taught that critical thinking is largely about the ability to interrogate claims. But perhaps the information environment now requires us to become equally good at teaching students to decide which claims deserve their trust. Ultimately, Descartes wanted his apples back in his basket, not scattered around the floor.

The word “currently” matters; it teaches them the theory of fallibilism. They’re practicing making the best judgment given their available evidence, even if that judgement turns out later to be wrong.
We often teach source evaluation by deliberately giving students dodgy sources (conspiracy theories, fake news etc.). But if that’s all we practice, we are essentially training suspicion.

a: Jen Weedon, Megan McDermott, and Sara Berger
q: Both described the same broad shifts: AI is not simply automating tasks, but reconfiguring the lived experience of work itself, with technical deployments currently outpacing organizational and human adaptation.

Across both cohorts, speed and productivity have become de facto organizational values; “good enough” is increasingly accepted as a new baseline; and productivity gains rapidly convert into higher expectations instead of the promise of returned capacity.

When discussing how they evaluated AI adoption, executives regularly defaulted to usage, speed, and efficiency—metrics that largely exclude the work of validation, translation, mentoring, coordination, and managing team anxieties.

Many of the very skillsets executives expressed fear of losing were already being performed, albeit often invisibly, by the organizational layer of middle management, whose future they were beginning to question. Organizations may value these functions in principle while relying on metrics that fail to capture them, and a tier whose primary contributions sit outside the formal measurement system will inevitably appear costly relative to its measured output.

This speaks to one of the questions that spurred this research, which is that decision makers and those implementing and experiencing their decisions do not always describe the same organizational reality. This is not necessarily because either is wrong, but because the instruments organizations use to understand themselves can make one cohort’s most valuable work difficult for the other to see.

These differences matter methodologically: asking organizations about AI transformation primarily through the language of strategy, productivity, and change management may systematically obscure some of its most consequential human effects.

Several groups observed that when organizations routinely accept LLM-assisted generalist work at 60% of expert quality, they effectively turn expertise from a baseline standard into a premium. Participants shared they believe that organizations still need subject matter expertise, but that the expertise is undervalued or reduced to its value for model training inputs.

Whether the emphasis on productivity in current metrics reflects an intentional definition of productivity as synonymous with success, or simply emerged as something that simply can be measured went unexamined. In other words, as reported by participants, organizations may be measuring what they can, rather than what matters, if the latter is even defined.

t: Two Concepts of Educational Liberty
q: Schools promise to help students think and act for themselves and yet constantly tell them where to sit and how to act. How can we make sense of this paradox? Especially in classical schools, how can we presume to provide an education designed to create free citizens while telling kids to sit down, be quiet, and memorize what we tell them to?

Within the school walls, liberty is neither the final telos nor a particularly effective means to achieving it. Rather, knowledge, virtue, and excellence are primary ends. In fact, a high degree of negative liberty can work in opposition to those ends.

Things are a little different in the classroom. Even a small amount of chatter or noise can disrupt every other student’s ability to learn. When it comes to an educational institution, it is necessary to create a smaller realm of “non-interference” around students in order to achieve the end goal of learning.

Thespians spend hours memorizing their lines and practicing their delivery. That they have learned to work within the constraints of a set play does not impede their liberty in the long run. Rather, in limiting themselves for a time, it expands their positive liberty.

The same dynamic—a short-term constraint on negative liberty in exchange for a long-term expansion of positive liberty—applies to all educational endeavors. A student acquiesces to quiet and recitation, so that they might learn to read and thereby access the entire corpus of Western literature. Students commit their math facts to memory and drill algorithms so that they can create the building and structures of their society. Education gives students knowledge and abilities, making reflective choice and self-command more possible. It prepares them to govern themselves.

Forming the free person” can become a warrant for coercion when educators claim privileged knowledge of a child’s true self. “For your own good” can quickly become a justification for enforcing the petty whims and desires of the educator, not the good of the student. Teachers must be wary that teaching children to “control their passions” does not create a permission structure to indoctrinate their own political beliefs or pass along their own therapeutic conception of the self. There’s a fine line between teaching and indoctrinating, but it’s a line we can and must define.

Schools, though, are discrete institutions with discrete ends. They exist, unlike legal frameworks, not to create a general societal framework that allows pluralism and individual choice, but to direct specific students to specific lessons. Some amount of paternalism is requisite. Moreover, teachers possess more proximate knowledge of each child, children themselves are not fully autonomous adults, and reading and numeracy are more defensible ends than a comprehensive political vision of the good life.

Ultimately, we must remember that a true classical education is one that emancipates a student’s mind from provincialism, assumed ideological consensus, passions, and their own insular interests to instead direct them towards virtue and truth. But genuine virtue requires the freedom of will to choose. And that is the reality we must remember not only to prevent a needful paternalism from metastisizing into authoritarianism, but also to ensure that students leave our building as self-governing individuals, recipients of a true liberal education.

t: Three Reminders From the First Week of School That I Really Needed
q: The week before students arrived, my mind map made it very clear that my mind was on things far beyond the classroom: school policies and leadership decisions, district directives and curriculum choices, and even broader thoughts around ongoing debates of AI, etc.

Then they did indeed show up and at once everything clicked into place: a good classroom is everything and students bring so much of that goodness in the door with them, in a way that no one not in the classroom can really understand.
That, after all, is something I can control as a teacher: staying present to the good taking place in the classroom right now, and Week 1 reaffirmed that continuously for me.

That said, I think it’s important to contextualize this enthusiasm a tad: I love reading student writing when they are writing in a way that is authentic and meaningful—and too often it feels like the gravity of our education system is pulling students in the opposite direction.

There are many ways to go about recognition in the classroom but underneath all those activities and strategies, I think, is the commitment to that priority: students deserve to feel seen in every classroom they step into.

t: This Can't Be Normal
q: Chanie works with school owners and organizational leaders who have built real, thriving businesses and still feel like they’re drowning. Not because anything is broken on paper.

Because of what she calls the invisible weight of leadership, the noticing, anticipating, and tracking that keeps running at 3am even when your systems, your team, and your checklists are all technically doing their job.
We get into why competence, the very trait that built your success, can quietly become the thing keeping you dependent on being needed.
It’s one of the clearest explanations I’ve heard for why telling an overwhelmed leader to just delegate almost never works.

We also talk about the rhythm she and her husband have built into their marriage, a standing Tuesday breakfast that’s pre-decided in calm and doesn’t bend to how either of them is feeling that week, and how that same structure applies to knowing when to close your laptop for the day.
People rarely change until the cost of staying still outweighs the cost of the alternative. Protecting your team from consequences keeps them from ever getting there.
Take the one thing keeping you up at night and walk it downstream, out loud, the way Chanie does with her client and the crayons, until you can see what would actually happen.

t: The Zoom Cycle
q: But there is a weakness hidden inside that strength. If you are naturally good at looking closely, you can become so absorbed in improving individual parts of something that you forget to ask what the whole thing is becoming.

That was when I started realizing that productivity was not really the problem. I did not necessarily need another way to organize tasks. I needed a better way to decide which tasks deserved to exist in the first place.
In fact, being productive can sometimes make this harder to notice because there is always evidence that you are accomplishing something. The day feels full. Things get finished.

If you never zoom out, you can spend years becoming efficient at things that are not taking you where you want to go. But if you spend all of your time zoomed out, you can become the person with a beautiful vision, an elaborate five-year plan, and remarkably little evidence that any of it has survived contact with reality.

That is also why I have become so interested in the idea of giving learning a destination. In the CARE Note-taking Method, I wrote that a learner can name a possible destination without pretending to know exactly where an idea will end up. The destination is meant to function as a compass rather than a contract.

When students understand that larger purpose, the smaller activity suddenly has somewhere to go. And perhaps that is one of the reasons so much learning disappears when school ends. Students become very good at completing individual trees without ever being shown the forest.

t: The Uncertainty Tax
q: The instinct is to treat this as a technology-adoption problem, which makes the issue a matter of keeping pace. That framing misses where the real cost lands. The disruption that matters most is not the arrival of any particular capability. It’s the condition of not knowing what comes next, and behavioral science has been measuring what that condition does to human judgment for a very long time.
The numbers describing worker sentiment aren’t just measuring the impact of AI today, they’re measuring the effect of not knowing its impact tomorrow.

The proof-of-concept theater that analysts described, endless pilots that never convert to production, is ambiguity aversion expressed as institutional procrastination. The reactive spending that outruns governance is the same aversion expressed as herding, the substitution of a peer’s apparent certainty for one’s own absent information.

An anxious workforce narrows, hedges, and conceals. Therefore, the psychological climate produced by the AI transition undermines the adaptive behavior the transition most requires, a self-defeating loop in which the disruption degrades the response to the disruption.

We don’t know” is corrosive. “Here is what we know, here is what we’re watching, here is the range we’re planning against, and here is when we’ll revisit it” converts a formless threat into a specified one the mind can prepare for. The reduction in stress comes from the specification itself, even when the news isn’t good.

Ambiguity aversion is most paralyzing when a choice feels irreversible, because the cost of being wrong is permanent. Structure AI commitments as options rather than bets wherever possible: staged rollouts, contracts that avoid deep lock-in, architectures that assume the underlying model will be swapped.
Certainty about the organization’s posture toward its people is available even when certainty about the technology isn’t.

t: The Siren Song of Marxism
q: In 1992 Francis Fukuyama published his bestseller, The End of History and the Last Man, celebrating what he thought was the historical triumph of liberal democratic principles over all other forms of political order. Times were heady, and many believed that the Marxist ideology that fueled the Soviet Union and other communist states had been demonstrably proven wrong and could be dispensed with on “the ash heap of history.” The hope was that communism across the world would wither, die away, and be forgotten forever.

In a poll from March 2025, conducted by the Cato Institute and YouGov, 62% of Americans aged 18-29 viewed socialism favorably; a shocking 34% of that same age group favored communism explicitly. What accounts for the enduring allure of Marxist ideology despite its empirically proven failures?

Historically, enthusiasm for socialist-communist ideology fades once students leave college, begin working, get married, and have children since these achievements tend to temper youthful fantasies filled with fuzzy promises. What happens, however, if this latest generation fails to join the adult world of responsibility, work, and family and continues to harbor the empty promises of Marxist ideology?

This coursework cannot be managed in simply one or two semesters. It needs to be a continuing inquiry across elementary and secondary school, and it needs to be fair and truthful in its treatment of the country’s achievements and failures.

As Solzhenitsyn wrote in his forward to the abridged edition of his Gulag Archipelago, If it were possible for any nation to fathom another people’s bitter experience through a book, how much easier its future fate would become and how many calamities and mistakes it could avoid. But it is very difficult. There always is this fallacious belief: “It would not be the same here; here such things are impossible” (xxix).

This current cohort’s ignorance of this history fuels their absurd claims about the efficacy and righteousness of communism. A serious treatment of communism’s history must be undertaken in high school, preferably during senior year before the students land in college completely ill-equipped to resist the siren song of their professors. Especially helpful on this score is reading memoirs and fiction by dissidents who survived.

Finally, schools should introduce a serious economics course that imparts financial literacy to the students. Thomas Sowell’s Basic Economics: A Common Sense Guide to the Economy is an excellent beginning. This is not a typical economics textbook full of dreary graphs and pie charts. Sowell is a masterful storyteller and surveys various economic policies and their observable fruits, focusing on incentives and results rather than dreamy declarations of hoped-for expectations.

The recent surge of Marxist ideology should concern everyone in the classical education movement. Our mode of education is liberal and specifically devoted to the students’ intellectual freedom. Studying history and economics provides a powerful antidote to much of this confusion, and classical schools should shoulder their educational responsibilities on this score.

t: The Practices of Cultivated Attention
q: Pick a feed, any feed — TikTok, Instagram, YouTube — and you’ll notice that what extends your session from the five minutes you intended to a loathsome hour and change is its unpredictability. What’s going to appear next?

To add insult to injury, the unpredictability of our feeds exists in a perfect and outrageous asymmetry: TikTok, Instagram, and YouTube are prediction engines, forecasting your behaviour with clinical precision. We cede our time, agency, and attention. They gain oracular knowledge of everything about us.
Silence isn’t the desired alternative, however. Silence is just empty, and it makes every sound that does appear even louder. What we want is sound that our students expect and understand.

When students understand what our proximity means, they don’t have to watch us all the time. The point is that as our presence becomes predictable, they come to know that our objective isn’t to keep a constant eye on them.

Routine is not just a source of comfort and security. In the twenty-first century, it is a temple retreat away from the endless rock concert of the digital world. Routine, in the classroom, is stimulus management.
It’s worth noting that routine is not monotony. What’s predictable is the container, not its contents. When our classrooms have a sense of routine, students arrive knowing what to expect.

Long before a student brings something to me, she’s predicted how I’ll respond, and decided whether it’s worth it. That calculus depends on how I handled someone else’s wrong answer a month ago, or what my face did when another student failed to finish a task.

t: The Greatest Work of Western Philosophy
q: The Republic is Plato’s most famous work of philosophy, and by far the most impactful. Imagined as a conversation between his mentor Socrates and various members of Athenian society, the Republic has influenced everyone from Aristotle to Augustine, Mussolini to MLK.

Whether you know it or not, you swim in the ideas contained in the Republic. From the Allegory of the Cave (which influenced everything from 1984 to The Matrix) to more complex ideas like those of justice, political legitimacy, and the tripartite soul, Plato tills the soil from which the Western intellectual tradition springs.
What is justice? Why should I be good when injustice benefits me? What makes a political regime legitimate? Who should rule? What is the purpose of education?

If you’re new to philosophy, this might feel frustrating. But the benefit of this approach is that it helps you identify the main struggles at the heart of any contemporary debate or political faultline.

Traditionally, the fullness of time has been understood as the historical moment in which Hebrew faith coincided with Roman order and Greek reason. The inheritance of Jerusalem, Rome, and Athens sits not just at the heart of Western Civilization, but at the very core of Christianity itself.

Of course, not all of Plato was accepted by the Church — while concepts like the immaterial soul and the insufficiency of earthly pleasure were retained, others like eugenics and the transmigration of souls were cast aside.
Just as a fish can’t recognize the water it swims in, we as modern individuals can’t recognize our own assumptions about the world. Plato helps remedy that.
Many readers of Plato are shocked to discover just how un-modern he is, yet at the same time find a sense of freedom in this revelation.

t: The Good and Goods of a Christian Liberal Arts Education
q: For advocates, these books are not only good, but somewhat easily identifiable. It is obvious to some people why our program should be like the title of Nadya Williams’s book and podcast: Christians Reading Classics. But for skeptics or the uninitiated, it may be unclear which books count and why.

The books and authors we assign all encourage contemplation and reflect attempts to touch “even remotely, the core of all things.” They may not all clearly apprehend the “hidden ultimate reason of the living universe, the divine foundation of all that is,” but they are seeking it. You can see it from Aeschylus to Arendt, from Hildegard to Hobbes.
Pieper is not worried about whether or not students need glasses, he is concerned about “the spiritual capacity to perceive the visible reality as it truly is.

At a Christian liberal arts school, or in a Great Books program, we want our students to be employable. But we don’t want to just teach them things to transition smoothly into the working world. We want to help them transition into a way of being in reality that rests on the divine foundation of all that is.

Last year several students in our program memorized Seamus Heaney’s poem “The Rainstick” after Malcolm Guite visited and charmed us all with it. We also have students involved in run club, or who sing in school choirs, or who study ceramics. Reaching out in contemplation is more than one type of reading or assignment or extracurricular activity.

The liberal arts are in decline almost everywhere, but they may be especially vulnerable within Christian higher education, because so many smaller Christian colleges and universities are closing. And, in many cases, the liberal arts are treated as ballast by universities in trouble.

And while across the country, K-12 classical education is on the rise, Christian colleges are not fully capitalizing on the opportunity presented. It is almost as though we have lost faith in what it is we do best.

They are interested in employment, but they are also interested in the nature of their existence and their relationship to things beyond the workplace. Exclusively vocational curriculum or exclusively secular pedagogy do not deliver these goods.

t: The First Weeks Back
q: We often fall into the trap of assuming that explaining and practicing a routine once or twice during Week One means it is “learned.” It isn’t. Routines, whether it’s distributing mini whiteboards, turning for a Turn and Talk, or silent transitions, require explicit instruction, live modelling, and relentless practice.

If the execution falls short of your standard, stop and rehearse it again. A good rule of thumb is to rehearse a routine up to three times in a single moment. If it’s still not quite there, give immediate feedback, move on with the lesson, and deliberately revisit the routine at the very next opportunity.

Secondary students sit through up to five or six different lessons a day, each with varying teacher expectations. Expecting them to master your specific classroom routines after 3-5 lessons is unrealistic. Routine practice isn’t a September-only task; it’s a long-term investment that requires practice well into the term.

Once students enter independent work (e.g. “Do Now” or ”You Do”), resist the urge to stay anchored to your desk. Consistent, active circulation is a non-negotiable practice throughout the entire academic year.
When you hold these physical boundaries consistently, students instinctually anticipate what mode of learning is about to happen simply by looking at where you are standing.

When a routine regresses, go straight back to modelling. Do not simply scold or demand better performance; pause the instruction, re-model the routine explicitly, and rehearse it again. Re-establishing a standard isn’t a failure or a waste of time; it is a necessary maintenance step that preserves your classroom culture.

When you allow one or two students to doodle, rest their head on the desk, or whisper while you are explaining content, you send a silent signal that full attention is optional. That non-compliance acts as a slow leak, more students will gradually adopt the lower standard, eroding the norm until you are forced to conduct a frustrating, high-energy class “reset” weeks later.

t: The Destruction of Community
q: Put simply, the more I’ve experienced of genuine community, and how it sustains people and builds power, the less enthusiasm I have for proxies.
And college football is an amazingly entertaining proxy of a genuine community; a perfect microcosm of the industrialization of human belonging.

Every institution began as a group of people who had high demand, high trust relationships and needed a name for what they were doing all day. Institutions use these bonds as a power source to preserve and enlarge the community.

The institution seeks to scale its capacity, resources, capital and prestige, all while trying to hold true to the original human connections that created it. But relationships and community scale poorly.
What happens when you scale something whose most essential component is relationship? Relationships become roles.
With the founding community now gone, only autonomous and interchangeable individuals remain. Any relational coherence now requires contracts.

At last, our journey is complete. We began with an institution that was built to preserve a fraternity of men. And we end with an institution that has only preserved itself by destroying the fraternity and isolating its members.

We live in a world of proxies. In family life, neighborhoods, schools, church, career, youth sports, government… everything. The same transformation of relationships into roles has permeated every connection.

t: The 5 Questions to Ask Before You Say Yes
q: A surprising amount of stress begins with a yes that should have been examined more carefully.
The problem is not generosity. A good life includes service, responsibility, friendship, compromise, and showing up when other people need us. The problem begins when saying yes becomes automatic.
This is why discomfort tolerance matters so much. Sometimes saying no feels worse for ten seconds and better for the next ten days.
Before agreeing, imagine the yes as an actual Tuesday afternoon rather than an abstract promise.
This is one of the most important things to understand about priorities. They are not only revealed by what you say matters. They are revealed by what receives your limited time.
Stoicism repeatedly brings us back to the difference between character and appearance. Character asks whether the action is right. Appearance asks how the action will make you look.
When someone knows that you do not agree automatically, your yes begins to mean something different. It means you considered the request. It means you believe you can carry it.

t: Subject, Object(ive)
q: It came into focus in 1949, when Ralph Tyler published Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction and argued that curricula should be built around clear, intentional targets (borrowing language from military contexts). Benjamin Bloom and others then gave schools a standardized vocabulary for educational goals, while the influence of behaviorism coached teachers to define success primarily as observable, measurable action – especially with the rigid formula of SWBAT (“students will be able to”).

We fundamentally believe that the purpose of education is not the production of isolated performances, especially on standardized exams. The end of education is the cultivation of excellence in the human person: a soul learning to know what is true, love what is good, and delight in what is beautiful.

The question, then, is not whether we have objectives, but whether our aims are ordered to a proper end. Backwards planning is genuinely helpful, provided we are honest about the end from which we are working backwards. It forces a teacher to ask where the lesson is going before she gathers materials, invents an activity, or writes a clever question. But if the endpoint is only a quiz or standardized assessment, the lesson bends toward something too small. Assessment itself must serve a higher purpose.

In our planning, we begin not with the state standard, not with the activity, not even with the assessment. We begin with the purpose of the discipline and the formation of the student. From there we work down to the course, the unit, the week, and finally the lesson.

A classical lesson objective should ask not only what students will produce or perform, but what they should know, what they should be able to do, and what proper loves or affections might be awakened. The teacher must triangulate these aims as she shapes content, activity, and assessment. In planning, the teacher must ask: What should this lesson invite students to love?

The Latin obiectum refers to that which is placed before the mind or presented to sight. In the medieval and classical philosophical tradition, an object is not an independent target existing apart from the knower; it is that toward which the power of knowing is directed. For this reason, a daily lesson objective cannot really stand apart from the knowing minds before us in the classroom. The objective exists precisely as an object for students’ understanding. In this sense, the objective and the learner belong together.

For public charter schools, they are a real obligation and, at their best, can hold schools accountable to a baseline of shared competence. But they should function as a floor, not a ceiling. A standard may say that students should identify a main idea, solve a type of equation, or explain a historical cause. It cannot finally tell us why a text stirs the soul, what order mathematics reveals, or how history might teach humility and judgment.

A good lesson begins not with an abstract statement, but with a concrete encounter: a beautiful sentence, a mathematical problem, a historical image, a scientific phenomenon, a story. Classical pedagogy begins with the particular thing itself and moves from there toward the universal. Students are trained, over time, to attend, notice, wonder, ask, and then understand and name. If we announce, “Today you will identify the theme of sacrificial friendship,” we may flatten the very experience by which students might have come to see it. We have given away the punchline.

t: Should the Bible Be Taught in Public Schools, No
q: Earlier this summer, the Texas State Board of Education approved a list of mandated texts, making it the first state in the nation to have a statewide required reading list. Out of the roughly 200 mandated works, about a dozen are Bible passages. The selections are spread from second grade through senior year of high school. The list takes effect starting in the 2030–31 school year.

Machen is worth hearing on this issue precisely because no one can accuse him of theological squishiness or embarrassment about the Bible. He gave his career, his reputation, and eventually his denominational standing to defend the full authority of Scripture. Why, then, did he so strongly oppose Bible reading in public schools?
Yet the way Texas plans to teach the Bible is to treat it as merely a part of Genre B—and not even the most important part.

Yet of the two competing messages—we should care about animals, and God cares about us—which are sixth graders likely to take from the reading, especially when it’s framed by the context of those other literary works?

Even if we were to set aside the problem of reading these passages in the context of other secular works, we still have the problem of unorthodox bias. As Machen points out, “The reading of the Bible is very difficult to separate from propaganda about the Bible.

It’s shocking that the same people who don’t trust public school teachers to teach history, literature, or science in a sufficiently unbiased way endorse having those same teachers teach interpretation of Scripture.

Using the words of Scripture—stripped of the requirement to see Jesus as Lord—to promote civics, character formation, or national heritage is a replacement of the biblical orthodox faith for generic civic religion.

The question that divides us isn’t whether the Bible deserves a central place in the formation of children—on that we agree—but whether a state curriculum is capable of giving it the place it deserves. Machen’s answer, and mine, is that it isn’t. We believe that the responsibility to teach God’s Word to children remains where God assigned it: with parents and with the church.

t: Recovering the Quadrivium
q: The language, literature, and history sequences look nothing like the local district’s, but the mathematics program is nearly indistinguishable from it. It seems that we have inherited a mathematics program designed for practical use and mental discipline.

But most classical schools today look to Dorothy Sayers’ 1947 lecture, The Lost Tools of Learning, for inspiration. Sayers proposed a curriculum based around the trivium, but she all but ignored the quadrivium. To recover the quadrivium we have to ask why we teach mathematics in the first place, and that means looking past Sayers to Plato and his successors, who answered it.
Mathematics education should not aim chiefly at practical usage or training the mind, but at turning students from the changing material world toward what is unchanging and true.

One of my geometry students told me that his favorite moment in the class came after completing a proof from Euclid’s Elements at the board and writing “QED.” When a student reaches that point and sees that the proof is valid and the conclusion could not be otherwise, he has encountered unchanging mathematical truth. He has been turned away from false images toward the things that do not change.

Children form an idea of what mathematics is long before anyone explains it to them. If their early experience is mostly drill and application, they will conclude that utility is the primary purpose. If they experience wonder and understanding, their minds will be purified to see the truth and will be better able to understand the true purpose of mathematics.

The aim of their educational philosophy is practical: preparation for college or preparation for the duties of life. In arithmetic, they recommend “omitting entirely those subjects which perplex and exhaust the pupil without affording any really valuable mental discipline.” Mental discipline was the criterion for content.

Every American body that stated the aims of mathematics named practical use or training of the mind. None of them said that knowing the object of mathematics, multitude and magnitude, is a preparation for philosophy. Until schools and teachers, my own school and myself included, can say this and teach mathematics accordingly, recovering the quadrivium will amount to rearranging the courses we already have.

q: Those are beautiful and significant claims. And if we’re going to make them, we ought to be willing to ask an honest question: Is it true, are we really doing it?

But the question about the efficacy of classical education is an empirical one. And answers to empirical questions can be informed by empirical research. Rather, Lewis points out that one must always both look along and at things, and because of that inevitably, he admonishes us to do the hard work of discerning if each way of seeing helps us see what is true. Sometimes, looking at might lead us to the wrong conclusions. Other times, looking along leads to self-deception. Still other times, both ways of seeing may be invalid or incomplete. Or perhaps both shed light on the truth in different ways, enabling us to see more clearly.

Teachers and leaders already spend a lot of time looking along. They experience head on the life of a school, interact constantly with students, and make innumerable everyday observations—all of which yield insight in the pursuit of excellence in their work. But looking along classical education is enhanced by the scientific work of looking at classical education.

Looking at can provide additional empirical ballast for practices classical educators have embraced primarily for normative reasons particular to the classical approach. For example, classical educators often make students practice handwriting and learn cursive mostly because cursive is beautiful and serves the aim of shaping students’ aesthetic tastes. That alone is sufficient justification, but evidence is accumulating that handwriting is beneficial to cognitive development.

But Peynaud countered that these old, revered cellar practices weren’t handed down by magic; they were themselves - at least originally - empirical, functional solutions discovered through trial and error. t: Latin in the Valley of Dry Bones
q: But the opinion that Latin is a living language, whether harbored among the professed ignorati or the honorary illuminati, is wrong. The Latin that classical educational programs aim to teach is dead, and no amount of wishful thinking or persuasion can bring it back to life.

Living Latin,” as a slogan, appeals strongly to the embattled psyche of the practicing Latin teacher, for whom the sentence, “Latin is a dead language” is now most often encountered as a challenge. From the earliest days of mass public education in the United States, Latin has been under constant pressure from advocates of more “relevant” or “useful” elective modern languages. As the case now stands, the accusation of “deadness” often seems to students, parents, and administrators alike, a sufficient argument to justify the exclusion of Latin from the curriculum.

Whatever judgment we finally render upon G-T, the new pedagogies, with slogans such as “Spoken Latin,” “Active Latin,” or “Living Latin,” possess one truly outstanding strength: they restore active linguistic production as both a method and a symptom of genuine linguistic mastery. In so doing, the more historically conscious of them recover traditional techniques employed from late antiquity through the Middle Ages and beyond.

The psychological appeal—who wouldn’t prefer the living to the “dead”?—is a tacit affirmation of relevance and usefulness as the criteria of value. Education must be “relevant”, is the assumption; old and dead things aren’t relevant; therefore, Latin shouldn’t be a part of education. If we deny that Latin is dead, this argument fails to land. But by evading the conclusion in this way, we allow the premise about relevance to stand and even seem to approve it.

A dead language is certainly not “relevant” in the same way that a living one is, but relevance (and utility) is not the only kind of value that education can offer. Relevance, as utility, is a transitory type of value: what is useful today may become useless tomorrow; what is relevant changes constantly. Classical education is committed to the pursuit of, not transitory, but transcendent value for our students, directing them towards Truth, Goodness, and Beauty and (as is often done) referring to these as transcendentals.

The demand for utility silently presses the other disciplines towards the point of transmutation. Through relevance, History becomes Social Studies, the Fine Arts become electives, Humane Letters become ELA, and the sciences (once known as natural philosophy) lose their investigative impetus and become repositories of useful facts.

A Neo-Latin novella, a TPR exercise, or an active conversation may serve as an intermediate object, just as a textbook does. Any such object may be employed as a means provided it conduces toward the proper object of study. Its legitimacy is instrumental; it should remove barriers, cultivate facility, and prepare students to enter authentic Latin texts.

t: Is There a Case for Copying
q: Just as novice scribes learned their art by copying the work of previous generations, young artists reproduced their masters’ paintings and apprentice craftsmen imitated expert techniques. Originality was understood to emerge from long familiarity with what others had already achieved. In this way, mimicry is a stepping stone to mastery.

Once you know to look for it, students’ books are often stuffed with what is very clearly copied verbatim from something their teacher has prepared. What can look like evidence of learning all too often turns out to be evidence of a teacher’s reliance on copying as a very poor proxy.

Students don’t have to select, organise, transform or retrieve anything. All they need do is hold a few words (almost never as much as a sentence) in mind for long enough to shift their gaze from board to page. The fact that students engage word by word instead sentence by sentence means their attention isn’t on meaning.

The negative effects of mindless copying are compounded for the children who most depend on us to make progress. Those with slower, or more untidy, handwriting, weaker spelling or difficulty tracking between board and page must devote all their available attention to keeping up.

Mimicry provides a crucial bridge between being unable to perform something and being able to perform it independently. By watching a teacher construct a sentence, students can be prompted to notice the interaction between subject and verb, why a word is rejected in favour of another and how ideas change in redrafting.

Copying gives novices a map through unfamiliar terrain, temporarily carrying some of the load while their attention is directed towards the features that matter. The risk is that students practise reproducing models without getting any better at independent production. Mimicry only works as a bridge if we expect students to cross it.
If we want students to notice patterns, rehearse procedures or imitate expert performance, copying may be justified, but only if we subsequently require them to do something with what they’ve copied.

There may be occasions when accurate imitation gives novices a safe first step into more demanding expectations but if we’re going to make children copy, we should be clear about how the activity will lead to more durable learning. If we can’t give a convincing answer, we shouldn’t waste their time.

q: This experience taught me that while miscarriage is common, it is never commonplace for the husband and wife who lose their child. Common does not mean “small.” A child was anticipated, loved, prayed for, and already given a place in the family’s future.

The husband cannot fix her grief. His first call is simpler and harder: to remain near her. He can say, “I am here. I miss our child too. You do not have to carry this alone.

Temperament matters. Some women process sorrow quietly, while some men need to speak. Some husbands feel the loss immediately; others begin to feel it weeks later. Neither spouse should make his or her manner of grieving the standard for the other.

Confession is appropriate where there has been actual sin. A husband who was harsh should confess his harshness. But neither spouse should transform ordinary failures into a secret explanation of God’s providence. We are responsible for the sins God reveals, not for causes we invent.

He should remember that physical recovery and grief do not follow the same timetable. The expected due date may be especially difficult. So may Mother’s Day, a later pregnancy announcement, or the birth of another child in the family or church. A wise husband remembers these moments and moves toward his wife before she must ask.

A grieving husband is not his wife’s savior. He cannot explain the providence, remove every fear, or call their child back from death. He is an undershepherd in the home, also in need of the Good Shepherd. Yet he can remain. He can listen. He can weep.

t: Go First 16, 2026
q: There’s a key theme from Terrie Noland’s contribution to Reading Isn’t Optional that we used to open September’s Secondary Literacy Commons (SLC) session: Go first, be an advocate, be a thought partner for planning and implementation. It’s written as guidance to school leaders. But the group took it as guidance for everyone in this community, whatever role they hold.
Co-creation without top-down accountability produces a well-built plan everyone is free to ignore. Top-down accountability without co-creation produces compliance that ends the day the pressure does.

Letting teachers surface concerns and push back during the planning process isn’t weakness — it is a strategy. The resistance that comes out in a planning meeting is the resistance that doesn’t derail implementation later.

Here is a belief that sits underneath a lot of resistance to supporting literacy in middle and high schools, rarely stated out loud: kids in grades 6–12 already know how to read, so my job is to teach my content area not reading. You cannot mandate your way out of that belief. It doesn’t respond to a new policy or a required training. It responds to influence.

You can require a teacher to sit through a workshop on morphology instruction. You cannot require them to believe it matters for their students. Getting from the former to the latter is the actual work of leadership, and it’s slower and more relational than most systems are built to support.

One of the clearest takeaways from the session’s reading on exemplary high schools was also the most uncomfortable: low levels of proficiency in literacy have been tolerated for too long. That tolerance isn’t usually malicious. It’s often rooted in genuine affection for students and a reluctance to hold them to standards they feel set up to fail.

The mindset shift that effective leadership requires: struggling to read may be how students arrive; it is not how students leave our school. Evidence-based literacy instruction needs to be visible at every grade level, not just in Kindergarten through 3rd grade. Leaders in middle and high school need to expect it, monitor for it, and build the conditions that make it possible.

Leadership doesn’t manufacture belief. But it creates the conditions in which belief becomes possible: the data that makes the problem visible, the training that makes the solution accessible, the structures that make the practice sustainable, and the culture that makes trying something new feel safe.

The central tension the group identified is between co-creation and accountability: co-created plans without accountability get ignored, while mandates without co-creation produce compliance that evaporates.
Co-creation and accountability must be paired: planning that lets teachers push back surfaces resistance early, but leaders must then hold structures in place when results are slow.

t: For All Teachers of Socratic Seminars
q: In my experience, high school Humane Letters teachers who are struggling to make their seminar discussions lively and sustained often think that the problems lie in the precise phrasing of their discussion questions, in the students’ intellectual abilities, or in the difficulty of the texts themselves. But not infrequently, a large number of much smaller and mundane things are piled up in plain sight around the classroom, figuratively and literally, if not choking then at least restricting the airways of good Socratic discussion.

In these and other not-quite-right table formations, the contiguousness is interrupted in a way that undermines the unity and collective nature of the seminar. If the teacher is seated away from the students, the message is silently conveyed that he is the sage and center of attention rather than the first among equals.

Students are generally prone to bring far too much STUFF to class, piling up thick binders, folders, textbooks for other courses, pencil pouches, notebooks, and sundry objects. The Humane Letters seminar should be a two-hour exercise in de-cluttering. Nothing should be brought to class that isn’t needed, and the only things that should be on the table in front of each student are a text, a writing instrument, and (optionally) a notebook or notepad for those inclined to write notes.

When I visit a seminar class, I can tell at a glance that certain students are unengaged and will remain that way for all two hours if let be: the ones who sit back two feet from the table, arms folded, leaning back at a 45-degree angle, legs extended and feet flat on the floor. This physical posture is both a sign of and a contributing cause of mental torpor.

These various activities should be thought of as being split up not 50-50 each day, but divided over a series of days, some of which are devoted entirely to seminar, and others to non-seminar activities. Breaking on the bell is artificial, kills the day’s momentum, and leads to further fragmentation.

Note that all seven of these items are physical, not mental. They have not to do with the intellectual work of understanding complex and rich texts, but with the material and bodily conditions of the class.

q: Except, think about what Thomas-Williams is saying here. She’s arguing that it’s not fair to have one common benchmark in English Language Arts, math, science, and social studies. She’s implying that it’s unfair to certain students to hold them to the same standards, because of course they could never be able to meet them.

Fundamentally, the fish-and-tree analogy gets the issue almost exactly backward. English, math, science, and social studies are not innate talents that some children possess and others do not, like a fish not being able to climb trees.
In fact, common assessments matter because students are different. Without them, it becomes much easier for adults to quietly lower expectations for students who are struggling.

A common benchmark says that regardless of which school you attend, how much money your family makes, or what your teachers expect of you, the state believes you are capable of learning the same core academic content as everyone else.

But beginning with students graduating in 2028, students will no longer have to demonstrate any particular level of performance on those exams. Instead, districts and schools will make up their own rules.

t: Curiosity in the Classroom
q: The instructional architecture and core principles of a Linguistic Phonics approach may increase the probability of effective and efficient learning of foundational reading skills. Similar activities and techniques used across programs may have less impact when inserted into curricular designs that differ in overall structure and core principles.

This is precisely what McGuinness offers with Linguistic Phonics. The content we teach (the code itself) doesn’t change, but how we perceive it does. Where Structured Literacy sees a duck, Linguistic Phonics sees a rabbit!

Unlike the traditional print-oriented phonics of Structured Literacy (SL), Balanced Literacy (BL), or Structured Word Inquiry (SWI), Linguistic Phonics designs instruction around clear, knowable boundaries that give novice learners a logical, coherent, and manageable framework. Within this framework, they efficiently discover how the code works at its entry level. Although this may seem like a distinction without a difference, when we organize instruction around speech—what’s known—and then attach letters—what’s unknown—we are anchoring our instruction in familiar territory.

Traditional phonics can place a heavy burden on a beginner’s working memory by introducing the code through graphemes rather than through speech. Taught backwards, from print to speech, the code’s relationship to spoken language and its underlying boundaries can become obscured.

The paradox is that starting with simple, knowable boundaries for learning the English alphabetic code builds the knowledge and skills needed to go beyond them to perceive the less knowable boundaries that define the code at its expert layers. Having these clear boundaries at the outset is what opens awareness and access in the long run.

Linguistic Phonics escapes from domains 1 and 2 early, but it can take far longer for traditional phonics to do so. Efficiency doesn’t mean rushing through phonics. It means being thoughtful about what we teach, why we teach it, how much explanation is necessary, and when students are ready to use their knowledge in authentic reading and writing tasks.

Teaching traditional phonics, including UFLI, is like keeping the training wheels on a child's bike too long. Linguistic Phonics offers them a pedal-less bike to push with their feet so they learn to balance faster and have time for reading connected text and writing.

We know that an understanding of the boundary conditions of our principles helps us decide what to leave out of our instruction as much as what to leave in. We streamline our lessons because we know that when it comes to phonics instruction, less can be more. But the goal is not simply to do fewer things. It is to make sure what we do is coherent, purposeful, and aligned with the way learning works.

t: Chapter House Books
q: Today, many families flock to alternative schools in large part, because they sense that something is missing in their child’s education. What is actually missing is Western Culture. More specifically, it is in the stories passed down that originate from the three great fountainheads of Western Civilization: Athens, Rome, and Jerusalem.

The Chapter House Series curates a beautifully bound cultural lifeboat for families, and I do mean beautiful. It is quite rewarding sitting down with my children to hold a clothbound hardback book, filled with beautiful illustrations and even more beautiful words. This is the type of experience that cannot be replicated with Dog Man or Captain Underpants. Aesthetically, the set is consciously anti-ephemeral and deserves a lasting place on the family bookshelf.

In Chapter 1, Joshua and Hannah Centers curate famous stories from Aesop’s Fables, Greek Myths, and European history. As they address in the companion essays, these works for younger children begin to form a moral imagination appropriate to a child’s age. This does not mean that the stories are dumbed down. The stories are meant to be read aloud, and it is in that magical process that a child’s imagination hitches onto the words to understand why it is dangerous to let a camel slowly into your tent.

It is in these stories that children receive more than just cultural knowledge; they receive Wisdom, precisely because the story encapsulates readily available truth faster than ChatGPT. In sitting down with my children to read these stories, I am amazed how the spoken word, which barely holds onto existence in small speech sounds, can lastingly temper a child’s heart toward Virtue.

In a culture saturated with depictions of mythology through the lens of Marvel, or indeed now with Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey, children interact with these stories visually first and narratively second. Even worse, their knowledge of myth is wrong or irreverent anachronistic (looking at you, Percy Jackson). The “Heroes and Wonder” selections offer a genuine reading with few pictures, for each child to develop an imaginative interaction with some of the oldest myths of our heritage.

Finally, many of these stories are too difficult for children to read on their own. The vocabulary at times is antiquated and polysyllabic in the best way. This provides, however, that other precious treasure of reading, the shared experience. What a wonderful gift for a child’s soul to be nurtured with beautiful stories read aloud by those they love.
