t: Bottling Up Your Emotions
q: We are in a society that is teaching youth, especially boys, that being vulnerable is a weakness and that feeling emotions is a recipe for failure.
That’s what isolation does. Your environment becomes more predictable and stops demanding more attention, so your mind shifts its attention inward. Your internal world gets louder.

Basically, changing your behavior when emotions happen so you can hide them, at least on the outside. Bottling things up, though, is more than that. It includes experiential avoidance — plainly avoiding the experience or the feeling — as well.

Before I begin talking about this, though, I want to introduce an idea: the perseverative cognition hypothesis. This is a framework that, in a nutshell, states that a physical stressor doesn’t need to be there to keep causing stress.

The thing is that burying your feelings not only impacts you as an organism, but also how you interact with others, your identity, how you perceive yourself, and, consequently, your own behavior. Bottling things up is then a channel for drift.
Cognitive reappraisal does something fundamentally different from avoidance: it changes our interpretation of a situation in order to change how it impacts us.
Honestly, I think “letting go” after reappraising is also valid, as long as letting go stems from a real acceptance of the situation rather than avoidance.
Remember, brushing things off is okay, as long as you really deem them unimportant. Otherwise, reappraise.

t: Before Classical Education, There Was New Criticism
q: Classical schools tend not to subscribe to the skills-based approach to English literature classes, in which students practice content-neutral linguistic tasks like guessing a word’s meaning from context, distinguishing denotation from connotation, or summarizing the main idea of a passage. Classical students are more likely to learn about the symbolism of water in The Miracle Worker, Scrooge’s character development in A Christmas Carol, or the theme of “atavism” in The Call of the Wild—in short, knowledge of literature.

At first glance, the definition of close reading might seem obvious: reading attentively, slowly, and carefully. But, while people have read books attentively for centuries, Guillory is focused on defining a practice belonging to a particular literary movement that emerged in the 1920s: New Criticism. According to Guillory, the New Critics’ novel and controversial approach to literature, eventually named close reading, “permanently transformed literary studies.

One distinctive quality of classical pedagogy is that it avoids historicizing works of literature. While students in a history class may consider how various events and trends shaped a primary source, literature teachers urge their students to remain focused on what’s in the text itself. Classical educators may be interested to learn that this practice has roots in New Criticism.

They believed literary works possess “organic unity,” meaning they’re internally coherent, with all parts contributing harmoniously to an overarching theme. They were formalists, meaning they believed that we can understand a book by studying its content, rather than needing to consult the author’s biography, historical context, or external statements about the work.
Learning about an author’s biography or a book’s historical context can be a distraction; it can burden the reader with assumptions and biases, narrowing the vision.

Borrowing from New Criticism’s formalism, classical schools steer students toward an understanding of authors as careful, deliberate artists who make choices based on what strikes them as good and beautiful rather than being unwittingly shaped by material or psychological forces. They help students to understand that part of what makes an artist great is the ability to transcend his or her context, and they avoid the troubling tendency to reduce authors to their immutable characteristics.
This was the contribution of the New Critics: making reading visible and therefore compatible with writing, discussion, and debate.

In other words, literature is great if it’s dense—if it’s rich and complex enough to invite intense conversation, lively debate, interpretive analysis essays, and other forms of close reading, often across decades or centuries. The Iliad is great, in part, because we’ll never quite settle our questions about the tension between fate and free will in the narrative, the antidote to Achilles’ rage, or what it means for the generations of men to be “as the generation of leaves.

Instead of the teacher having the sole authority to speak, our classroom is designed as a place where everyone in the room has something valuable to say. Attentive listening needs intentional practice.
Listening awareness gestures like these give the speaker observable indicators that they are being heard by the group.

A month into the school year, I have observed that when students are sitting in their assigned seats, they often do not realize that someone is addressing the class. I do not want to interrupt students mid-share to quiet down those who are still talking with their tablemates.

Since classroom discussions are not in a circle and often require time to think before responding, having a visible cue might discourage side conversations. The expectations for listening would be the same and it would be clear who is speaking.

Teaching students how to listen to each other is the most important skill needed for a democratic, respectful classroom. Attentive listening is the foundation for all forms of group discussion like Socratic Seminars and book clubs or literature circles.

t: An Invitation
q: You can do anything you want as long as it is virtuous,” he read aloud, clearly searching for the right way to kindly engage me in a corrective conversation about my classroom décor. We were, after all, preparing for the upcoming meet-the-teacher night.

He listened graciously, then asked me to consider what we should truly be pointing our students toward. He asked me to reflect on the nature of goodness and whether virtue is relative; if it’s up for individual interpretation. He didn’t shame me; he didn’t give me the directive to change what I had displayed; he simply invited me to have a conversation.

I was humiliated and even a little angry. My entire management structure had been questioned, and my classroom was always well-managed. Not for the last time, I felt out of place and small and wondered if classical education was a good fit. If I was a good fit.

In retrospect, I see that even the revamped motto was still gimmicky; after 14 years in a classical network, I know there are better ways to establish appropriate learning conditions and draw students’ attention to virtue. I know that I don’t need to rely on gimmicks, mottos, or slogans. The invitation my headmaster extended to me that afternoon to consider something deeper left an impression.

The aim of a classical education is to habituate students toward the pursuit of excellence, and our work as its practitioners is to help the students answer the questions, “Who am I and what am I to do with my life?” Our call is not merely to create lifelong learners; it is to form souls.

I felt out of my depth, and my visceral response to the discomfort of being challenged, of being a novice, was defensiveness, bordering on contempt. But because I was invited into the conversation, because I was asked to actively participate in dialogue about reality, something in my soul expanded. And that, the invitation to behold reality, is what we have the privilege of offering every day as classical educators.

t: Across the Trojan Plain
q: While Eratosthenes criticizes Homer for prioritizing amusement over instruction—myths and monsters over hard data—Strabo responds that Homer’s myths and poetry were in fact instruction, in something more profound than basic facts: a “primitive philosophy.” Geography is philosophic because it asks why landscapes matter. Time and again, Homer illustrates how the places he describes influence human choices. The role of the Trojan Plain in The Iliad is a prime example.

The plain is not just the setting for The Iliad. It creates the visibility, mobility, and vulnerability that influence how warriors maneuver and earn glory. In some ways, the flat plain is egalitarian, while in others it reinforces rigid class structures.

But the openness of the plain exposes the success and failure of both heroes and common soldiers alike. Its unbroken views erase privacy and leave nowhere to hide: no forests to disappear into, no ridges to mask movement, no caves to regroup inside.

These Lycian and Cretan commanders both recognize that leadership does not bestow a license to hide, but rather a responsibility to visibly represent the community in the heart of the fray. Sarpedon recognizes that the very danger of being the exposed battlefield on the plain presents an opportunity to show courage, and thus to demonstrate that his aristocratic status is not just inherited, but earned.

In an unobstructed space devoid of natural boundaries, Zeus imposes his own. His ability to produce an impassable barrier amid emptiness illustrates that even the ground heroes stand on is subject to divine power.

Hector correctly credits Zeus for the Trojans’ success thus far, but he fails to recognize that later, in retreat, the same open terrain that facilitated his advance could bring defeat, as eventually it does.

Here, Achilles shows a lack of sophrosyne (moderation, restraint) as he transgresses two sorts of boundaries: the physical river that guards Troy and, in the act of polluting and attacking it, the cosmological boundary between humanity and divinity. As the literal embodiment of the landscape, Scamander rises to halt the hubris-driven fury of the greatest mortal warrior.

In The Iliad, Homer shows how the Trojan Plain is far more than a backdrop to the war. Its openness creates possibilities that shape battle strategies, paths to glory, and the limits of human ambition. Time and again, characters who understand the possibilities the landscape presents are able to exploit them, while those who do not, suffer the consequences.

t: 2 Ways to Fail Your Child
q: There are two ways to fail your child, and they move in opposite directions. You can fail by keeping too much out. You can bring up a child so isolated from anything that goes against your faith that by age 18 she has no means of coping with a world that doesn’t agree with her. When she meets a compelling false idea, how will she know how to wrestle with a doubt if those have never been discussed? How will she be able to explain what she believes to someone who disagrees with her if she’s never had practice doing it, or even seen anyone else do it?

You can also fail by letting too much in. You can be so afraid of being labeled as one of “those weird Christian parents,” or want to keep dinner peaceful, that you end up treating your faith like a private matter not worth mentioning. You avoid filtering what your kids watch or listen to because you’re not going to be one of those legalistic religious types. So you skip the hard conversations. But kids get the hint: Christian faith is an optional preference. It’s not important.

Now, thanks to smartphones, every child in America is basically living in Manhattan. They may not walk through Times Square, but they scroll through it on their phone. All culture is right there in their pocket.
The Bunker creates hothouse flowers. These kids look healthy in temperature-controlled, windless environments, but they aren’t ready for the weather of the real world.

The sociologist Christian Smith found that the single strongest predictor of a teenager’s faith isn’t youth group attendance or church involvement. It’s the religious seriousness of his or her parents. Children rarely surpass what they observe growing up.
The Bunker and Bubble strategies both fail, though for opposite reasons. The Bunker gives a child truth without grace. The Bubble gives a child grace without truth.
You’re not banning the movie, but you’re not blessing it either. You’re teaching your child to think. This is how you build spiritual antibodies.

When you know the operating manual of the embassy, you don’t have to panic when your kids bring home confusing questions about identity, sexuality, meaning, justice, or morality. Instead of shutting down the conversation out of fear like the Bunker parent, or ignoring the moment like the Bubble parent, you can slow down. Affirm the longing behind the question. Identify the distortion in the cultural answer. Point toward the hope that Jesus is putting the world back together, and your child with it.

t: 1MW No. 323 Always Say Less
q: Every time you speak, you teach people how closely to listen next time.
Restraint signals self-control. The person who can listen without rushing to speak commands more attention when they do. Their words carry weight because they have been selective with them.
When we can't stop talking, people may wonder what else we can't control. And the longer we talk, the more opportunities we create to say something we wish we hadn’t.
Like a credit score, your contribution score is a history that precedes you. People decide how much attention to give you based on what you have done with it before.

This is an uncomfortable idea for those of us accustomed to proving our value by contributing more. It is difficult to accept that we may be training people to pay us less attention—including when we finally have something essential to say.
The cost of unnecessary words isn't just the time they consume. It's the attention our future words no longer receive.

In the absence of such rules, those of us who are less permissive with tech are left to attempt to explain violent or sexually explicit concepts to our children, rehearse together what to do if they see something troubling, and ask God to protect them when we aren’t there to shield them from evil. It’s exhausting.
I’m thrilled about the landmark settlement. But the cat is still on the loose, and parents are tired of chasing it.
Tech advocacy on behalf of kids is missional for those who follow Christ, a matter of loving not just our own families but our youngest neighbors.

Pursue beauty and truth as a family. Nothing reveals the emptiness of scrolling like real-life adventure. Walk the nature trail. Create some art. Read a good book out loud (including to older kids who may not admit it but still crave story time).

We did this at my kids’ school when we found out students were sometimes on screens instead of socializing during downtime.

t: When Candor Is Kind
q: Soft-pedaling messages and communicating indirectly feel kind in the moment because they avoid friction and maintain relational harmony. In many cases, though, such relational diplomacy simply defers the cost of ambiguity to a later time.

Candor is not kindness when a leader feels relieved after the conversation and the other person feels flattened, even if the content was true.

t: The Karpman Drama Triangle: How to Stop Playing Victim in Your Own Team
q: Almost every week, he would tell me some version of 'I'm the only one fighting for the team.' Every problem we raised to him quickly turned into his problem, and then somehow, into his personal mission.

Karpman wasn't studying office politics or leadership philosophies. Not at all. He was actually studying fairy tales and stage drama. Karpman noticed that basically every story — whether Little Red Riding Hood, soap operas, or even your family's Thanksgiving dinner — features the same three characters, or 'roles', showing up over and over again.

The Rescuer. This is the one who pops in to 'fix things' like it's their problem. But in most cases, the rescuer tries to rescue a situation that doesn't need rescuing at all. He tries to help people who didn't really ask for help.

You rescue your team by lowering the bar. They feel like victim of your low expectations. You get frustrated with that, and become the persecutor. The team gets frustrated, disengaged, and burnt out. Rise and repeat.

The value of learning this framework is to become more self-aware and team-aware. You want to be able to detect when you're playing one of those roles of the drama triangle, and how you get out of that trap.

t: Make Explicit Connections to Prior Knowledge
q: We can make it more likely that students will assimilate new ideas with relevant existing knowledge . . . by stating explicitly what the connections are when we explain things.

Activating prior knowledge is NOT 'vague reminders' or 'generic starter activities.' Instead, we need to 'actively recall and use relevant knowledge before connecting it to new learning' and then 'explicitly [link] prior knowledge to new content.'

I cannot assume that students will make those connections even though it was reviewed at the beginning of the year or because they learned it last year. Too often I have watched students struggle to 'find' or remember what they have learned, or they have inaccurate or incomplete memories of the learning.

t: Knowledge Hiding Degrades Sense-making and Decision Quality
q: Executives get the systems view partly because their role demands it, and partly because holding it protects their position. Almost no one below them gets to see how the pieces fit together, or where the real leverage points are, until leadership decides it's time to share.

If an organization wants people who think in systems rather than just execute, it has to distribute the systems view rather than hoard it at the top. That's a much harder cultural shift than picking the right framework.

t: How I Give Technical Feedback to an Engineer Who's More Technical Than Me
q: Pretending you reviewed the code is worse than admitting you didn't. And once you get caught faking depth once, every future piece of feedback from you gets discounted. That's the real cost.

The instinct is to compensate by forcing some kind of technical analysis anyway, hunting for something clever to say about the code itself. The moment you improvise an opinion on something you can't defend, you're not giving feedback anymore, you're gambling with your credibility.

GitLab and Jira generate more signal about how someone actually works than most managers ever look at. Merge rate, review time, MR size, comments given and received, lines changed, deployment activity. None of it requires reading a single diff.
Before every feedback session, I collect input from whoever is closest to the work. When I bring that feedback into the room, I say exactly where it came from. I don't present it as mine.

What actually works is being honest about where your own view ends, and building a system that fills in the rest instead of hiding it. Metrics tell you the shape of the work. The people closer to the code tell you the substance.

t: FLMOP 14, 2026
q: If we want students to act in a certain way, we need to tell them what that is. Doug Lemov calls this the 'means of participation': quite literally the means by which students are participating at any given point.
Unfortunately, if the students heard the instruction, then they are already acting on it, and are unlikely to hear and properly assimilate the means of participation.
This is called Front Loading the Means of Participation, or FLMOP for short, and it's an extremely powerful way to create a classroom culture which is calm, quiet and efficient.

It's not guaranteed to work: FLMOP is a kind of behavioural nudge that gets students closer to doing the thing you want them to. Any teacher can do it, and in the majority of cases it will make a significant difference.

t: Don't Blame the Scripts

t: The Biscuit Story: A Lesson in Leadership From the Antarctic
q: Shackleton, without ceremony, handed Wild his "one & only" breakfast biscuit. When Wild refused it, Shackleton told him it would then be buried in the snow uneaten.
He later wrote that "all the money that was ever minted would not have bought that biscuit," and only someone who had also starved could understand what the gesture truly cost.
It is important to note that Shackleton was not directing his men from comfort while they suffered. He hauled the same sledges, ate the same rations, and slept freezing in the same tent.

This is the difference between symbolic sacrifice and genuine sacrifice. Leaders who perform gestures that look selfless but cost them nothing never earn the trust that goes to leaders who actually pay a price.
Shackleton did not gather the others to announce his generosity. He simply gave Wild the biscuit, one exhausted and starving man to another.

The leadership lesson worth remembering is that people will follow a leader through extreme hardship and adversity if they believe that leader shoulders the same load and confronts the same challenges as they do.

t: Pedagogy of the Oppressed is not about Pedagogy
q: Freire wrote about adult literacy among politically marginalized populations in 1960s Brazil. His concern was oppression, political consciousness, and emancipation, not how a ten-year-old learns fractions, algebra, or chemistry.

Just because a teacher explains photosynthesis, this does not mean the concept of photosynthesis gets deposited into a child's brain.

The learner has to attend, interpret, connect ideas to prior knowledge, retrieve, rehearse, and reorganize memory into his existing schemas. The learner has to stay cognitively active throughout. Regardless of the instructional method.
The better metaphor is the apprentice. The master demonstrates, explains, instructs, corrects, models, and gradually reduces the amount of instruction and support.

I want teachers to drop this guilt. No evidence has shown that explaining a concept clearly and directly harms students or oppresses them. Someone simply asserted it, and the repetitive narrative made it feel true.

t: Why is learning to read hard?

t: When Consistency Becomes Conformity

t: The Leadership Knowledge That Complexity Demands
q: What matters in school improvement? Ultimately better outcomes for students. Upstream of this is improving teaching, and upstream of that is improving leadership.

But schools are complex systems, characterised by features such as emergence, unpredictability, self organisation and historical influence. In such conditions, knowledge of the specific system within which we work is vital.

However a leader can know their school intimately and still misjudge a decision, still miss what's actually driving their own reasoning, still fail to spot a pattern they've already lived through once before. Closing that gap takes something broader than local knowledge.

I don’t want kids to have to be lucky. I don’t want children’s futures determined by the toss of a coin or the roll of a dice. Their futures are here, now, and urgent.
As the principal of a school with now more than 70% of our pupils in receipt of the Pupil Premium, I feel this keenly. It is a weighty responsibility.

And getting it right is about helping children make progress and doing well academically. It’s also about many other things, laced together in a complex, embroidered, richly woven tapestry of how glorious school can be.
I truly believe that getting a grade 4 or 5 or above in English and mathematics is the gateway to a world of possibilities for children. It flings open doors that would otherwise be tightly shut.

For flying me to Germany with my peers in Year 9 on an exchange to stay with a lovely family. For arranging for me to go even though we didn’t have enough room in our house for my exchange partner to come and stay with us in Birmingham.

t: Always Honor the Past Before Explaining What's Next
q: Amid change and transition, people go through an emotional stage of letting go of the old before they can commit to the new. Leaders who miss this essentially ask people to break ground on something new before they’ve finished with what came before.
They recognize that people were invested in the last effort. Team members showed up for it, staked their careers and reputations on it, and built relationships around it.

Honoring the past before diving into the next thing provides definitive closure and allows people to feel good about their efforts. This is even more important if the transition to a new objective follows a failure or a leader’s departure.

Even when the past effort didn’t achieve its goal, leaders can find something worth honoring in it. Lessons learned, skills acquired or sharpened, relationships forged along the way, and values demonstrated are prime examples.

This step isn’t a courtesy. It’s the foundation the next chapter will stand on. Leaders who skip it will likely find distracted team members still processing what came before and unable to fully commit to what lies ahead.

t: You Can Always Give Them Five More Minutes
q: After a wonderful afternoon on the playground, they told David it was time to go and he shouted back, "Just five more minutes, Daddy." And they relented as they always did. They just didn't know it was the last time.

There's a last time you change a diaper. There's a last time you get to speak with them. There's a last time you push them in a stroller or walk them to school or drive them to their summer job. There's a last meal, a last hug.

The reason it surprises us is that we don't know when...and because we love them, we love life so much, it always comes too soon. Which is why, when our kids ask for a few more minutes, for one more hug, for a ride, for anything, we should find a way to give it to them.

David's boundless energy and love were a gift to his Papa and Daddy and all those who knew him. David loved to play at this park-a little boy racing to climb and swing under the watchful eyes of his Papa and Daddy.

t: What Self Respect Looks Like When Nobody Is Watching
q: Self respect is easy to talk about when life is visible. It is easy to keep your standards when people are watching, when your effort will be noticed, when your discipline has an audience, or when doing the right thing also makes you look like the kind of person you want others to admire.
Nobody knows whether you kept the promise you made to yourself that morning. Nobody sees whether you returned to the work after becoming distracted.

Nobody knows whether you told the whole truth when a smaller lie would have protected your image. Nobody sees the moment you could have taken an easier path without consequence and quietly chose not to.

These private decisions rarely feel important while they are happening. There is no applause attached to them. They do not immediately change your reputation, income, appearance, or position in life. Yet they slowly shape something beneath all of those things: whether you trust yourself.
Not thinking highly of yourself all the time. Not pretending to feel confident. Not protecting yourself from every uncomfortable truth. It is living in a way that allows you to believe your own word.

t: We Owe Them More
q: The thing I remember-I will always remember it-was the eye contact. When adults saw each other, we stopped and looked each other full in the face. "How are you?" we asked.

The question was not really about being remembered. It was: Who are you responsible for? What are you doing with your time and energy that matters to someone besides yourself? Who has a claim on you? What do you owe?

I discovered how enormously difficult teaching is and how badly we prepare people to do it. Before long, I was writing again, this time about schools, curriculum, teaching, and what children need from the adults charged with educating them.

My colleague Yuval Levin has spent much of his career thinking and writing about the institutions of American life, and one of his most memorable insights is that institutions are not merely things that exist as platforms for our personal performance. At their best, they are molds that form us.

Police officers and other first responders ran toward people they did not know because those people were in their care. Duty was not an abstraction. It meant: Someone is depending on me, so I have to go.

We have become accustomed to describing what is owed to us and less likely to ask what we owe. We treat institutions as things to exploit when they serve our purposes and despise when they do not. The question cannot be: What is wrong with everyone else? It has to be: What is mine to take care of?

t: Fathers and Sons 2: Your Depression Is Contagious, And Your Son Caught It
q: Even when he tries to conceal his emotional struggles, his children may still experience their effects. A father's anger can contribute to anger in his children. His depression can increase their risk of depression.

A meta-analysis of more than 7.1 million father-child pairs found that paternal depression was associated with a 42 percent greater risk of depression in children. When the father had a diagnosed depressive disorder, the risk was 65 percent higher.
Susan Schwartz calls a father's emotional struggles his "shadow." If a father does not confront his shadow, it can interfere with his ability to meet his son's needs and be a good father.

Boys need fathers who can embrace "the benefits of active participation in the lives of their sons." Left without this participation, a father may be physically present but emotionally withdrawn leaving the boy with father hunger.

Boys need fathers who can allow themselves to be "positive, loving, relating, nurturing, warm." Left without nurture fathers, sons experience a void in their fathers and learn to associate masculinity with emotional withholding.
Left withdrawn and disengaged the son may cry out for years for his father's love mixed with feelings of hurt, anger, disappointment and hope that dad will someday love him.

t: Working Literacy Back Into the Secondary Classroom
q: Literacy initiatives cannot thrive if they are only birthed from a district office, a consultant's slide deck, or one coach's calendar. The work needs local leadership from people who understand the culture, the schedule, the personalities, and the actual students in the building.

When an initiative is built mostly by ELA teachers, even with the best intentions, it can unintentionally communicate that literacy is still an English department project. When the work is shaped by disciplinary specialists across the building, it communicates that every content area has texts, language, questions, conversations, and ways of making meaning that students deserve access to.

The organization we partnered with offered a month-long training for literacy leaders. We chose to send the literacy coach, one administrator from each school, and a representative from special education. If I could do it again, I would train the entire literacy team.

Teachers can feel the difference between an initiative that has a thoughtful path and one that is being built while they are walking on it. When the adults leading the work are still trying to understand where it is going, the rest of the staff often experiences the initiative as unclear or scattered.
If I could change one major piece of the plan, I would spread the courses across the three years instead of having each cohort complete all three courses in a single year.

Slow initiatives give teachers time to understand the purpose behind the strategies. It lets departments adapt the work to their disciplines instead of performing generic literacy activities that feel disconnected from content. t: Why Leaders Must Get Good at Arguing
q: From disagreements over the right strategy to adopt to heated recriminations following a project failure, conflicts are a regular part of business life. But most leaders and teams view conflict as a negative that should be avoided at all costs.

Developing a sustainable approach to building resilience in the face of change and conflict first requires leaders to understand that workplace dynamics are deeply interconnected. How leaders process stress and tension is impacted by the specific contexts they're operating in: the people with whom they work, and the different ways those individuals process their own stress.

A group's anxiety typically comes from fears of survival and doubts over whether people truly care for one another. If these anxieties are suppressed, this can lead to interactions that seem polite enough on the surface but are emotionally distant or inauthentic.

Failure can make us feel incompetent and ashamed, so when something goes wrong, energy is often spent diverting the blame. A leader might criticise others for resisting their ideas, when the truth is the leader actually feels insecure about their own abilities.
The key is to get beyond the "what happened" part of the conversation to tackle the "how did we feel" dimension and explore "what these feelings made us do to each other".
Discontent, arguments and disagreements are all part of daily work and leadership. If everyone saw things the same way, we would lose our diversity, creativity and innovation.

t: What Does It Mean to Lead an AI Agent?
q: It doesn't have human motivation, judgment, or organizational awareness of its own. And an AI agent can't be held accountable for what it does. Only a leader can grant an agent the authority to act.

An AI agent is closer to an organizational capability with delegated authority. What a leader permits it to do, and forbids it from doing, is the leader's entire job. Everything else follows from that.
What leaders must decide is whether to allow them to alter a process, send external communications, weigh in on personnel decisions, spend money, or commit the company legally.
Good leaders don't just tell the agent what it should do. They tell it what it must never do. The second instruction usually matters more than the first.

A leader can't watch every agent action. It is up to the leader to inspect the outcomes. That means building checkpoints, quality thresholds, escalation rules, exception reporting, and measurable outcomes into the system before the agent ever starts working.

Leading an AI agent, then, is less about management and more about architecture. It requires leaders to think upfront about outcomes, authority, and consequence in ways that traditional delegation rarely demands.
An agent will simply execute with whatever authority and boundaries you gave it, including the ones you forgot to set.

t: The Man Spectrum
q: Not every man needs to be about bourbon, hunting, Carhartt jackets, and Super Duties. I love bacon, IPAs, deadlifting, and home improvement projects as much as the next guy, but the reality is that masculinity has a much broader range than we think of it today.

With many young American men struggling, masculinity as likely to be described as "toxic" as anything good in the media, and a variety of dodgy online influencers who are actually leaning into the idea that toxic masculinity is good, it's important for our society to put forth a positive, aspirational, attractive vision of masculinity that men actually want and can imagine themselves being part of.

The lesson from Paul is that any positive vision of manhood must be capacious enough to include men from every socio-economic and occupational class. It shouldn't be out of reach for the poor, but neither should being rich or elite be seen as incompatible with being a "real man.

Not everyone needs to act like a monk, but men need a mission, a purpose to pursue, a sense that they matter. They need to have something for which they would sacrifice their comfort or in some cases even their lives if necessary.
The lesson here is that it is incumbent on men to build up the next generation under them and successfully pass the baton. This is something we've failed miserably at as a society.

Today, a relational orientation and nurturing style are seen as hallmarks of a feminine style. It's true that women tend to be stronger in these traits, but the lesson here is that these are tools men can have in their repertoire as well.

They need a society that provides a man spectrum they can put themselves on, one also with a standard to meet and excellences to aspire to, and which provides validation and honor to those who measure up to that.

q: The presence of norms in school is inevitable—there is little we can do about it. However, the nature of these norms is within our influence.
Norms are the unwritten rules of conduct that influence behaviour and learning in school (& society). They are so powerful that they often override more formal policies and rules.

Our perceptions of norms arise predominantly from the observation of others. And so, the best way to influence norms in school is to raise the visibility of those behaviours and attitudes that we want others to emulate.

Normative messaging is more effective when it emphasises what we want to happen, rather than what we don't. Chastising a class by telling them that most students didn't do their homework can reinforce rather that deter such behaviour.
100% adoption is the ultimate lever—even a single dissenter makes it easier for us not to follow along. When we see one person picking up litter, we might consider doing it.

Normative messaging is most potent in novel situations. Once norms have taken hold, they become increasingly hard to change. This is why it is worth taking time to get things right in the early days of establishing a class.

t: 1MW No. 322: That's Not What I Meant
q: The greatest bottleneck to understanding is not misunderstanding. It is confident misunderstanding.

Nothing is more costly than confident misunderstanding, especially when we know how to turn conviction into action. When that conviction rests on an error, our strengths begin working on its behalf: talent solves the wrong problem, strategy organizes around the wrong reality, and execution accelerates in the wrong direction.

Every consequential conversation carries two signals: what they are trying to convey and what you are trying to convey. If either one is lost, whatever happens next is built on only part of the available reality.
Listen and Speak belong together. Listening means making it safe for their signal to emerge. Speaking means having the courage to let your signal emerge.
Reflect and Confirm belong together, too. Reflecting means using your words to unlock their intended meaning. Confirming allows them to use their words to translate yours.
This is simple, but it is not simplistic. It is simplicity on the other side of complexity.
The point of the Signalist Circle is not merely to be understanding. It is to understand accurately enough to act on the same reality.

t: The Power No One Has to Give You
q: Murphy and his associates had studied 18,000 managers across 562 organizations and identified just over 1,000 people who demonstrated exceptional leadership ability. One of the findings was deceptively simple: people perceived as true leaders are those who value their own competence more than any externally bestowed affirmation.
Authority is conferred while leadership is developed and honed by people working to uplift others.
Leadership is not about men in suits. It is a way of life for those who know who they are and are willing to be their best to create the life they want to live.

Authority matters. We give people formal authority because societies and organizations need ways to make decisions, allocate resources, enforce laws, and hold responsibility. But authority is not the same as agency.
Agency is our voice. Our attention. Where we spend our money. What we are willing to question. Whom we invite into a conversation. What we create when what we need does not yet exist.

Control is inherently precarious. If my sense of power depends upon maintaining my title, keeping people aligned with me, accumulating more money, defeating an opponent, or ensuring that others behave as I wish, I am forever at risk of losing it.
This power is impossible for others to take without our consent. And it is what our current moment is asking us to reclaim.
It was never something another person could bestow upon us. It is ours to develop. And ours to choose.

t: Making the Audience the Hero in Your Presentations
q: In any presentation, the speaker is not the hero. The audience is. Presenters naturally feel they are the stars of the show since they're the ones on stage. But it is the audience that must adopt the ideas.
The presentation gets built around the audience's experience with the content, not the presenter's rationale, logic, or argument.

A leader announcing a reorganization, for example, doesn't open with the reasons behind the shuffle. They open with the tension the team members feel, such as uncertainty, capacity, and trepidation about what it means for them.
Instead, they arrive with one clear and useful gift, an insight, a framework, a solution, and hand it over to the audience almost immediately.
A good presentation then alternates between what is (the status quo) and what could be (the vision of something better). Duarte calls this shape the Sparkline
This alternating structure is what keeps the tension alive long enough for the audience to feel the stakes, rather than simply being told about them.
When the presenter steps back and hands the audience the pen, the story becomes theirs to finish. The presenter simply points the way.

q: If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative

If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative? Our superintendent wisely said, when we founded our center, that technology was the fulcrum, not the focus.

The difference with AI, I would say, is that it has three components that the rest of technology didn't have: speed, or acceleration, we've never seen a technology be this quickly adopted and this fast-moving; lenses, people looking at this technology through all different lenses, with AI everyone has different viewpoints; and ownership, with technology it was pretty clear who owned the learning, teachers were in control of things, with AI we don't have ownership clearly defined.

I realized that teachers were doing a great job of redesigning their curriculum and instruction with schools as they currently are and with AI as they currently were, and I said this is not going to continue down this path, I really need to make people more aware of what the future of school could be.

There's a bill in New York, the FOCUS Act, that wants to ban all internet-connected devices in grades kindergarten through fifth grade. We had all of our fifth graders in Scarsdale do an independent research project, and they had to do internet research. What do you do if they have no technology?

I use an AI simulator. I show them how it constructs a sentence word by word. I also show them that it's not really thinking. It's pattern matching. I think that is so important, not just for teachers to understand, but when you hear about students engaging in relationships with AI, thinking of that as a person. Here's what's happening behind the scenes, it simulates that you're talking to a person, but in fact you're talking to a broken calculator.
There should be a national initiative that really creates almost a series of lab schools and a dedicated research institution to focus on AI and education.

t: Instruction That Improves Itself
q: In traditional classrooms, the quality of the teacher determines the outcome far more than the lesson plan or the curriculum. The only real lever is training: observe a teacher, coach them, observe again. It is slow, it is expensive, and every gain evaporates the moment that teacher leaves.
a good teacher motivates students because they are right there. Software has none of that, and a product students don't want to use is worth nothing no matter how good its instruction is

If you are using whole class direct-instruction, your advanced students are bored, the instruction lands well with the middle 50% of the class, and your struggling students are confused. When you use AI for tier 1, your advanced students rocket ahead because they are no longer limited by what the rest of the class needs, your middle 50% do just fine with about the same amount of repetition as whole-class, and now your struggling students get direct support from the teacher every day.

An AI Observer that digests all sessions each day, diagnoses where instruction breaks down, and files the problems. Next. Simulated students supplying the sample size a single small school can't. Next. Agents that pick up those filings from the Observer and fix them, so a problem found Tuesday is gone Wednesday. This Fall.
After several years of refinement, 70% of those students passed the assessment we gave immediately afterward. Seventy percent is our bar for AI instruction.
Suppose the system gets half a percent better each day. Over a 180-day school year, that's roughly two and a half times better than where it started.
None of this removes the teacher. It removes the part of the job that was never a good use of a human being: delivering the same explanation to the same confusion for the thirtieth time.

Every school on earth already runs uncontrolled experiments on children. A new curriculum, a new schedule, a teacher trying something different third period, these are experiments, just unmeasured ones, and nobody calls them that. What's different here isn't that we're experimenting. It's that we're measuring, and that a change that hurts students shows up in the pass rate within a day and gets pulled.

t: Contradictory Demands Are Everywhere in Teaching
q: There's the learning-facing pull, the kid who's stuck, the group that needs support right now. And there's the adult-facing pull, the parent email, the colleague who needs five minutes, the team meeting where you're supposed to show up. Both are real, both are constant, and neither one goes away because the other one is loud.

Contradictory yet interrelated elements that exist simultaneously and persist over time, elements that seem logical when considered in isolation but irrational, inconsistent, and even absurd when juxtaposed.
A dilemma is a one-time choice, weigh it, pick, move on, the choice sticks. A paradox is different because any choice is only temporary.
Poole and Van de Ven made this point back in 1989: contradictions like this are built into how organizations function, not signs of dysfunction to be engineered away.

Sundaramurthy and Lewis later showed the same pattern in corporate governance, boards that tried to resolve the control-versus-collaboration tension once and for all, in one direction, consistently did worse than boards that kept both in play.

A vicious cycle, you pick a side defensively, dig in, and treat the other pole as the enemy. A virtuous cycle, you accept the tension as real and permanent, and you move back and forth between the poles on purpose instead of freezing into one.
Instead of asking someone to defend a decision, ask what they set aside to make it, and whether they noticed doing it.

q: My problem was that I'd confused independence as an educational aim with independence as a teaching method. I wanted students to become independent interpreters and assumed the best way to achieve this was to get them interpreting independently. As experts, we've automatised the pattern matching involved in interpretation. Because this is what we think happens in our own heads, we believe that if only we can teach students the skill of interpreting, they'll be fine. This, however, is a classic case of expertise induced blindness.
It's not that interpretation isn't skilful, it's that the skill can't usefully be separated from the knowledge that makes it possible. The more we know, the better we are at interpreting texts.

All too often, our approach is inadvertently elitist. An approach intended to promote independence can privilege precisely those students who arrived with the greatest literary and cultural resources.

The goal here is 'gapless instruction'. Every time we rely on knowledge we haven't taught, or ask students to perform a complex process without ensuring they possess its component knowledge, we create a gap.
Genuine independence rests on internalised knowledge. If our goal is to teach children to interpret independently we must give them enough knowledge to think with.

t: Do the Work

When a word is particularly abstract, such as 'hope', it may be more beneficial to assign an icon, symbol or widget to it.

t: What Programmers Get Wrong About AI
q: The problem is that many of the people making sweeping forecasts about the future of work have spent their careers doing one particular kind of work, the exact kind of work that AI got good at first.

AI has been strongest in the parts of programming with clear inputs, clear outputs, and fast feedback. It has been less reliable at deciding what the company should build, why it should build it, and what tradeoffs it should make.
That kind of work does not grade itself. There is no test suite for materiality. There is no clean answer key for professional judgment under uncertainty.
The question that best indicates which jobs will be affected most is: How quickly and objectively can we tell whether the work was done well?

But AI is an input, not an owner. It cannot carry the accountability of choosing a strategy, hiring an executive, committing capital, or deciding which stakeholder interest should prevail when they conflict.
We should take technologists' warnings seriously while recognizing that their experience with code is not a complete theory of the future of work.

t: The Hidden Cost of Thinking You Know Someone
q: What we believe affects what we notice about someone. Our brains can only consciously process a tiny fraction of the information around us at any moment.

There's a good chance it's the comment that fits what you already believe about her. This is a type of confirmation bias: we see whatever confirms our initial assumption about a person, while tending to miss evidence that points the other way.

If you already think of him as highly capable, you might see the question as evidence of good judgment: he knows when it's worth getting another perspective. But if you've begun to doubt his capabilities, exactly the same question might strike you as further evidence that he lacks independence.

Over time, small daily differences can compound and create very different paths for a person. One path might lead to micromanagement, low motivation, and slowed development; the other might build toward opportunities for growth, advancement, and agency.
When we notice we've become very sure in our beliefs about someone, it's often worth creating room to check for other interpretations.
The point is to hold these beliefs lightly enough that you can still recognize the signs pointing in another direction, toward a bigger set of possibilities for this person you care about.

In March, AI was treated as a novel governance object requiring its own dedicated apparatus. In September, it is folded into a screen-time policy and governed by the same developmental logic that districts are applying to cell phones and tablets.

In effect, prohibition just offloads the complexities of AI into off-campus spaces. It removes supervision and guidance, and leaves unsupervised use in place, calling on parents to do the real work of AI literacy. This is the irony. Parents calling for bans of technology in school are creating more work for themselves.

In a somewhat stretched analogy: my neighborhood is now host to packs of elementary and middle school students riding motorized bicycles that hit 40 miles per hour, but our current system asks them to become proficient at driving only when they turn 16.

Screen time is (sort of) governable. Minutes can be counted. Devices can be closed. AI and its impact on learning cannot so easily be counted or closed down. The policy governs the thing it can measure and sets aside the thing that cannot.
The children on those motorized bikes are not waiting for a license. They are already in traffic.

t: Teaching about 9/11: History and Memory
q: Two years before the National September 11 Memorial Museum opened, The New York Times reported on the fraught debates over its creation, when the attacks were still fresh and survivors and their families strongly debated what should and should not be included in its exhibits.

Museums are about understanding, about making meaning of the past, said James Gardner, who oversees the nation's legislative archives, presidential libraries and museums. A memorial fulfills a different need; it's about remembering and evoking feelings in the viewer, and that function is antithetical to what museums do.
But knowing where I was and how I felt is not the same thing as knowing all about what happened on September 11 and why.
I think now of every war memorial I ever yawned through on a class field trip, how someone else's past horror was my vacant diversion and maybe I learned something but I didn't feel anything.

History distances us from the past, in both time and space. That distance can be useful, giving us the perspective to analyze events more clearly. But it can also make it harder to feel the human cost, raising a thorny question: Is it even our job as history teachers to close that gap, to invite students into empathy as well as analysis?

Memorials remind us that history is lived experience, not just a set of facts. Holding space for remembering, for feeling, and for seeing the humanity in others is part of how we nurture the kind of citizens our democracy requires.

t: Mastering the Pause: Compassion and Positive Intent
q: Do your best to assume positive intent as your default setting. Not because everyone always gets it right. Not because difficult behavior should be ignored. And not because compassion means abandoning boundaries or accountability.

We know that we were doing the best we could at that moment. But when someone else's mistake impacts us, we do not have access to their internal experience. And our brains can quickly fill that gap with the worst possible interpretation.
But when we get completely hooked by those stories, it becomes much harder to see what might improve the situation. Compassion can give us enough freedom to look again.

My hope is that you take away from this series that the Power of the Pause is not simply about becoming calmer. It is about creating enough space to choose how you want to think, respond, and show up, even when other people do not behave exactly as you hoped they would.
You do not have to excuse everything. You do not have to agree with everything. But you can practice giving yourself and others a little more grace.

Performance also suffers when people have completed a prior task under low time pressure. It is only when people have completed the prior task under high time pressure that their subsequent task performance is enhanced.
For teachers, the takeaway isn't just add a timer. It's a bit narrower and more useful than that: a task doesn't end for a student's attention just because you've announced it's over.
An unannounced stop catches attention mid-task, which is exactly the unfinished state Leroy's data associates with residue. Staged warnings give students time to start wrapping up before the switch.
A small, definite last move, reached while time is genuinely tight, is closer to her high-pressure completion condition than to an unhurried finish.

The point worth holding onto is the mechanism, not the exact wording: a transition in activity doesn't guarantee a transition in attention, and the more predictable and closed you make the boundary, the less of Task A a student is likely to be carrying into Task B.

t: America's oldest school model may be its future September 3, 2026
q: For much of the 20th century, Catholic schools took the children of factory workers, dockworkers, and new immigrants--Italians, Irish, Poles, Puerto Ricans--and gave them an affordable education that launched them into the middle class and beyond.

In fact, while many school systems remained closed, more than 90 percent of Catholic schools reopened for in-person instruction in the fall of 2020. Families noticed. Catholic schools once again earned a depth of trust that could not be manufactured.
For the first time in a generation, federal policy is not merely tolerating Catholic education. It is creating room for it to grow.
At a moment when many institutions struggle to answer basic questions about purpose, Catholic schools possess a coherent vision of the human person and an understanding of what education is for.

The challenge facing American education today is not simply the transmission of knowledge--AI is making information ever more accessible. The qualities that will matter most are those that cannot be automated: judgment, self-command, compassion, and courage.
Catholic identity and mission are non-negotiable; the traditional parochial school model should not be.
For decades, Catholic education has been defined by closure announcements and questions about survival. That story is over.

t: All Call: What Are You Woodenizing Right Now?
q: Woodenization is first and foremost an attitude that says, I assume that if I want my students to do something well, it's my job to be clear about how to do it.
The name comes from Coach John Wooden, who famously taught his collegiate athletes how to put on their socks and tie their shoes on the first day of practice each season.
When Woodenizing, teachers are wise to think in terms of two categories: Smallies, stuff that can be taught once, with total clarity, and then reinforced thereafter. Smallies are matters of habit.
Biggies, stuff that needs to be taught multiple times over a time period in order for students to better understand how to do it well. Biggies are matters of skill.

The key question of the Woodenizer is: what learning-conducive behaviors would I like all of my students to master? From there, pick a few smallies and one biggie that you most want your students to master, and start breaking them down with as much clarity and simplicity and power as you can.

The information was still complex, but the doctor's explanation reduced the extraneous cognitive load. By lowering the cognitive load, Olivia could focus on the meaning instead of decoding technical language.

t: What Does It Really Mean to Teach English?
q: We teach pupils to take marks on a page and turn them into voices, people and worlds. We ask them to sit beside the dying Mercutio, walk the streets of Victorian London, hear the wind on the Yorkshire moors and recognise the simmering fury beneath the politeness of a Jane Austen drawing room.

Yet, creativity does not emerge from emptiness. We make new ideas by combining, adapting and transforming what we already know. A pupil cannot play imaginatively with the conventions of a sonnet without first encountering sonnets.

Teachers resist the imposed knowledge-rich curriculum while often reproducing its assumptions. They criticise prescription but return to Shakespeare and the canon when asked what matters. They defend creativity while invoking a relatively traditional conception of literary culture.

q: Research shows that young children whose parents read them five books a day enter kindergarten having heard about 1.4 million more words than kids who were never read to. Those words equate to knowledge, and, thanks to cognitive science, we know that background knowledge is key to learning and connecting new knowledge.

The more knowledge a child starts with, the more likely she is to acquire yet more knowledge. She'll read more and understand and retain information better. Because knowledge, like Velcro, sticks best to other related knowledge.

An actual web that has more connections and links will be much stronger than a web with fewer and will do a better job at catching bugs. The web that has very few attachments is more likely to break and simply doesn't have the same ability to trap any bugs that may fly into it.

Additionally, children who are read to regularly at home tend to develop positive attitudes toward reading and learning, and tend to associate reading with happy, pleasant experiences. This practice helps classroom teachers by alleviating the need to convince reluctant children why reading is important.

q: This discovery of yours will create forgetfulness in the learners' souls, because they will not use their memories; they will trust to the external written characters and not remember of themselves.

The specific which you have discovered is an aid not to memory, but to reminiscence, and you give your disciples not truth, but only the semblance of truth; they will be hearers of many things and will have learned nothing; they will appear to be omniscient and will generally know nothing; they will be tiresome company, having the show of wisdom without the reality.

The person with a vast library, in one sense, has much knowledge available to him, but he does not himself know anything unless he takes it upon himself to inscribe that knowledge not only in books but on his own soul.

What your average person knows today often doesn't rival what a sixth grader knew in the 1940's. We rely on something else, something external, to contain the knowledge for us and we are content to look it up only if and when it becomes relevant and, in most cases, we release that information back into the void about 15 seconds later.

Knowledge is a prerequisite for wisdom and wisdom is a prerequisite for prudence and prudence is knowing what is right and true, understanding what one ought to do in light of that knowledge, and then actually doing it when the time for action comes.

t: The 3 Reasons Smart Leaders Produce Weak Strategies
q: Even an MBA teaches you ABOUT strategy. It never has you build one.

SWOT, Porter, Blue Ocean: everyone applies the same tools to the same market. Filling in a canvas feels like progress, but no framework makes the hard choices for you. So the framework produces a document, and the real questions stay open.

Goals for every department, so nobody feels left out. “Growth,” “efficiency” and “innovation” all at once, with no choice between them. Nothing the company decided NOT to do. A plan everyone approves because it commits nobody.

You take last year’s document, or a template from your previous company. You update the numbers, refresh the market slide, add the current buzzwords. You fill every box: mission, SWOT, pillars, initiatives, KPIs. The deck looks complete, so leadership approves it. Six months later, nothing has changed in how the company operates.
Here’s a quick test. Take your current strategy document and ask: “Could a competitor paste their logo on this deck and change almost nothing?” If yes, you have a template, not a strategy.

t: Teaching in an Age of Tech-Created Distraction
q: And so our devices, browsers, and even now some of our most basic tools have become heat-seeking missiles for our attention.
Then as now, the pedagogical juice has to be worth the technological squeeze.
In 2003, it wasn't crazy to have a student individually follow a link to watch an educational video in RealPlayer. In 2026, I would never direct an individual student to watch a video on YouTube.
For two decades, I believed that edtech's ability to empower and motivate kids was worth the distractions and the junk software. But I'm not so certain anymore.

t: Can We Settle for Assimilation?

q: The data simply do not support the social media/smartphone hypothesis. But even those in authoritative positions who reject the media/smartphone hypothesis have so far almost uniformly avoided examining my alternative hypothesis, that a major change in how we do schooling, instituted by the Common Core State Standards, increased the stress of schooling and thereby elevated the rates anxiety and depression among school-aged kids, especially teens.
As I have said many times before, no adult would willingly accept a job that is anything like the schooling we impose on our kids. We would all see it as a job from hell.

Every year, when summer vacation from school begins, rates of anxiety, depression, pediatric mental health admissions, and teen suicides plummet, and every fall, when school starts again, those rates go up again. By some measures they double.

Common Core dictated that teachers, principals, and whole school districts would be evaluated based on the students' scores on standardized tests covering a narrow range of curriculum, especially math and literacy. The inevitable effect was reduction in teachers' freedom to adapt what they were doing to meet the needs and interests of students and truly engage students intellectually, and an increase in boring, time-wasting drill.

t: The Truth About Fiction
q: The core problem with this assumption is that it reduces growth to knowledge and limits knowledge to a particular type of knowledge. Having restricted growth to increasing one's knowledge, it then flattens knowledge to mean only technical information; the assimilation of new data; the storing of facts -- all things nonfiction works are generally designed to help us do.

The Philosopher Peter Kreeft suggests that the human soul has three prophets: the intellect, the imagination, and the conscience. These prophets reveal to us three aspects of reality: truth, beauty, and goodness, respectively. Nonfiction generally appeals only, or at least primarily, to the first of these: to propositional truths, understood as external facts.

One of the reasons fiction is indispensable to the serious reader is that it makes up a substantial part of the culture-expressing and culture-shaping body of literature. Works of fiction are a gateway into understanding culture -- whether that of others, or your own.

Speaking in great generality, nonfiction is adept at filling and forming the head (the rational; the intellectual), while fiction is adept at forming the chest (the sentiments, the orientation, the conviction). If we wish to avoid men without chests or bodies without heads, it's a good idea to include both fiction and nonfiction in our diet.

People wonder why the novel is the most popular form of literature; people wonder why it is read more than books of science or books of metaphysics. The reason is very simple; it is merely that the novel is more true than they are.
Fiction stands as something of a bulwark against this trend by preserving that wholeness and presenting it to us in a complete story. And stories are powerful -- they move us and help us remember.

q: When Kaya became Chancellor of DC Public Schools, she inherited a district in a free fall — the lowest-performing urban school district in the United States, 40 consecutive years of enrollment decline, a graduation rate under 50%, and 29 data systems that didn't talk to each other.

Kaya's core move was refusing to treat her constituents like children. When schools had to close, she didn't hand the community a decision — she handed them a proposal and then put her team's data next to the community's data.
Her point: people are reasonable. We act like they're crazy, but they're only "crazy" because we don't give them the information.

In order to give her changes their best shot at becoming permanent, Kaya built a five-point plan simple enough that anyone in the district could recite it, because memorability is how change survives past the leader who started it.

t: The Most Dangerous Moment in Any Decision Is the Moment You Feel Sure (leadwithkelly.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: A man knocked on my door in San Francisco and handed me legal papers. I was being sued for the people I had just hired. The ink on their offers was barely dry.

There was a problem I could see clearly. The company was full of brilliant software people and almost no one who understood the machines. You cannot predict when a machine will fail if no one in the building knows how it works.
So I was about to hand the best mechanical engineers in the world to a company that believed mechanical engineers were a thing of the past. Two tribes. Each was certain the other was beneath them.

The people were everything I said they were. It was beside the point. The outcome was never going to be decided by talent. It was going to be decided by a culture I had watched reject the idea of them before they ever arrived.
That is the trap. Certainty about the one thing you can measure becomes certainty about the things you cannot. Will the market show? Will the cultures merge? Can I hold this together on will alone?
Now, when a decision gives off that clean, confident hum, the part that says, "At least this choice I know for sure," I have learned to treat it as the warning, not the green light.

q: For the entirety of the 20th century, across the developed world, each generation of humans was a bit smarter than the last. The best evidence we have for this is the Flynn effect. Humans have steadily improved on IQ tests over that century, where each decade the average test-taker improved by about 3 points.
We can’t attribute much of these gains to what was happening in schools. There’s just no evidence that the quality of education has made a substantive difference.
Either there was a broad conspiracy across almost the entire developed world to ruin schools while also somehow making adults decades out of school dumber, or the cause isn’t actually in schools.

Here’s the story I’m telling. For a long time, as the world became more complex, that complexity caused humans to think harder and think more and made us smarter. Then, a second trend began: cognitive automation displaced some of that thinking, slowly at first but then faster and faster.
I’m not saying school is useless. If school disappeared tomorrow, student achievement would plummet. Covid was an unfortunate but illustrative natural experiment to prove that point.
Horace complained over two thousand years ago about kids these days, and we haven’t stopped since. Every generation has argued that we are declining from some golden age in the past.
We won’t build a better education system by looking to the past. It will be something built, brick by brick, by humble, knowledgeable, passionate, and persistent educators.

t: Sisyphus Versus the Flywheel September 1, 2026
q: In the Sisyphus Model, a city's schools get so bad that the mayor or the state takes over. They appoint some brave new leader who has the authority to concentrate decision-making power, adopt new systems, and bring in new people. With luck, they can push student achievement up the metaphorical hill.

Celebrations ensue, and the hard-charging leader steps out of the picture. But over time, the political winds change, the new systems weaken, old habits return, and the rock starts rolling back down the hill.

Under the Flywheel Model there is no one hero. Instead of centralizing power under a single entity or person, a city devolves much of its decision-making authority to individual schools and school networks.

City leaders measure results, let successful schools grow, and close schools that consistently fail to attract families or produce results. With luck, successful schools grow and replicate, new schools learn from what works, and the lowest-performing and most under-enrolled schools close.

As I describe these models, I have real-world examples in mind. Both models have good stories to tell and have produced genuine successes. But which one would you bet on to make the most progress over time?

For most teachers this is the right spend. Three days covers the overwhelming majority of absences, and generic beats specific because you cannot predict which day you will be out.

For the typical teacher this is renting a solution to a three-times-a-year problem. You will pay $90 to use it twice. The math almost never works against a $30 tub you build once and reuse for five years.
A beautiful binder with vague content is worse than an ugly page with good content, because it looks complete and is not. The sub will read one page. Make it the right page.

t: How to Start as a Primary ECT September 1, 2026
q: Starting as an ECT in primary is a daunting feeling. Suddenly, you go from being a student teacher in someone else's class to having your own class.

As an ECT, you should not have been given a class with particular behavioural issues (and if you find out that you have been, this is a huge red flag about the school). However, any class in a mainstream primary school will have its issues.

It's best to be really firm on rules and routines at the outset when the children are sussing you out and considering whether to push the line. It's quite easy to relax a little later on if you have been too insistent on something.

I am a strong believer that behaviour should be regarded as part of the curriculum and needs to be taught just like everything else. In particular, good behaviour in school involves a whole set of individual behaviours which need to be taught.

By the end of the first week, some of your more enterprising students will be testing boundaries. It's important to reinforce them at this point because it will only get harder in weeks 2, 3 and thereafter.

This is a recipe for burnout and, in my opinion, a nonsensical way to run a school. Primary schools vary hugely in the amount of shared resources they have and their attitude to using them so you will need to scope this out quickly.
The basic idea is simple. You tell children how you want them to participate before telling them what you want them to do.

t: Experts Shape Meaning (admiredleadership.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: The last word doesn't refer to holding the floor last or making the last point. Nor does it mean advocating last or even speaking before the discussion ends.

For a true expert, having the last word means being the one whose framing survives the discussion. It means that when the conversation is over and people depart, the frame they carry with them is the expert's interpretation.
The discipline is taking the complex and noisy and making it simple and clean. Done poorly, it is a crude oversimplification. Done smartly, it adds an instant clarity to the room.

A room full of people can spend an hour debating a topic, but a true expert closes the exchange by saying, in effect, "Here is what actually matters." That statement is what persists as the rest fades away.

Experts often signal that an issue is settled, describing the terrain so clearly that further arguments feel unnecessary. An expert has failed if they let a discussion trail off into ambiguity or let someone else plant the frame.
The right to define what just happened isn't handed to anyone. Experts earn it, one accurate frame at a time.

t: Changing Your Inner Conversations (leadershipwithatwist.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: What we tell ourselves matters. Our internal conversations influence how we feel, how we behave, how we communicate, and ultimately what happens next.
After you pause and separate the facts from the story, the next step is to notice the story itself. What are you telling yourself about the situation?
In leadership, our internal narratives can have a tremendous impact. We may tell ourselves someone does not respect us, a team member should know better, a mistake is unacceptable.
Once we can see the story we are telling ourselves, we have more choice about whether we want to keep carrying it forward. That is personal empowerment.

You cannot always control what happens before the pause. You cannot control how another person chooses to behave. But you can become more intentional about the story you carry forward and the person you choose to be within it.
The next time you notice yourself getting emotionally stirred up, take out a piece of paper and write down what you are telling yourself. Get it out of your head and onto the page.

t: Being Available Is How I Lost A Year (summermulder.substack.com), September 1, 2026
q: I never finished the Skool community. We ran it free for our clients, extra support on top of what they were already paying for. I'd launched it with a few modules and about a hundred members had joined.

It sat on my list for over a year, sliding forward one square at a time, and I don't think there was ever a single day where I looked at it and decided not to do it. It just kept losing to whatever was in front of me.

I think about it more than the failures that cost money, because it's such clean evidence of a pattern that ran my entire working life. The thing only I could and should do got pushed. Every single time.

There was something else underneath it too, and it took me a long time to see. I wanted my team to know I cared as much as they did. If they had an idea for an email campaign, I wrote it that same day.

It shows up identically. You have two contractors and a VA. Every question comes to you. Every decision waits on you. It looks like support until you notice every decision is still sitting on your desk.
What finally changed it was one sentence I said out loud on a Thursday afternoon. It was urgent for them in that moment. That didn't make it urgent for me.

t: Back to School: We Are All Teachers of Language September 1, 2026
q: We all teach language, sometimes explicitly and analytically, always implicitly and informally. For all formal education is conducted in and through words, through language.

Our language is not just a means of “content delivery”—it is always a co-subject, the background and scenery, the substrate, the foundation upon which the structure of the arts and sciences is built, even as other academic and intellectual and moral and aesthetic topics appear to be the sole concern.
In teaching literature, we are teaching language about characters and actions and dramatic choices and the detailed, subtle texture of existence as perceived through the human senses.

When language is strong, beautiful, clear, and used to reveal the true and move hearts to right actions and hard choices, human beings accomplish great deeds. Worthy works are wrought. Cultures rise to new heights.
As Confucius puts it in the Analects, “…when language is used incorrectly, what is said is not what is meant, what should be done is left undone…and the people stand around in helpless confusion.

t: AI in Education #13: Five Things I Learned from Joe Liemandt about Motivation, Data, and the Future of the Teaching Profession
q: His reasoning is about motivation, which Joe reckons explains 90% of Alpha's success. He points to Laurence Holt's 5% problem: the finding that many EdTech products' positive results are only positive when you exclude 95% of the students who fail to engage with the product.

In their online sports academy, the kids do their two hours of academics at home in the morning, and only get a QR code for the afternoon session at the athletics facility if the system says they have genuinely mastered the work. Joe's line is that if he relaxes that constraint even slightly, the mornings collapse.

Alpha set up a programme called "100 for 100" where a student sits a test several years below their age grade and gets $100 for getting 100%. Then they take the test for the next grade up, and if they get full marks, it's another $100 coming their way.
You do not tell that child they are in third grade and years behind. You tell them their rate of learning is excellent, because it is, and because that number gives them a reason to keep going.
He thinks learning science has forty-odd years of good ideas and no microscope, because the effect of any intervention is swamped by the messy classroom it happens in.

It takes roughly 11 hours in their maths facts app for a third grader to reach fluency. A fourth grader who has that fluency gets through the year's maths in about 30 hours. A fourth grader who does not takes about 61.
He will not, because if the adult is not delivering the academic instruction, the word gives parents the wrong picture of what they are buying.
